the-modern-ai-agent-2023.name: The modern AI agent
the-modern-ai-agent-2023.definition: A software system built on a large language model that perceives its environment, reasons over open-ended tasks, and acts through tools in a loop.
the-modern-ai-agent-2023.bottleneck: Before the modern AI agent, machines could not perceive, reason over, and act on open-ended tasks in a loop, because no model could flexibly convert between language, perception and action, and there was no practical way to train or steer such a model.
the-modern-ai-agent-2023.leap: Instruction-following LLMs wrapped in a reason-act loop with tool use (2022-23: ChatGPT, ReAct, function calling) turned a text completer into a general task executor — a capability jump, not an incremental accuracy gain.
the-modern-ai-agent-2023.prior_state: Chatbots and task-specific ML systems: models could complete text or classify inputs, but could not follow open-ended instructions reliably, use external tools, or chain reasoning and action toward a goal.

in-context-learning-2020.name: In-context learning
in-context-learning-2020.definition: Few-shot conditioning phenomenon documented with GPT-3 (2020): models perform new tasks from examples in the prompt alone.
in-context-learning-2020.bottleneck: Before in-context learning, adapting a model to a new task required gradient updates and labeled datasets, because behavior could not be specified at inference time.
in-context-learning-2020.leap: GPT-3 (2020) demonstrated that a frozen model performs new tasks from examples and instructions in its prompt - behavior programmed in natural language at inference time.
in-context-learning-2020.prior_state: Fine-tuning per task; zero-shot transfer limited to narrow formats.

sources.title: AI Paper Review: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (Wei et al., 2022), Sections 1-2

verification.notes: Q1 attack partially lands and is recorded: the capability was latent in the model rather than created by the prompt format - the paper's own framing is that reasoning 'emerges naturally in sufficiently large language models' via elicitation. The flip scored is an access flip (impossible to obtain from a frozen model before, obtainable after), which stands. Multiples test on Q3: no independent co-discoverer of the paradigm itself; Min et al. (2022) is coeval analysis, not a multiple. Mediation attack via GPT-3 (the paradigm arrived inside the GPT-3 paper/artifact) answered by the components discrimination recorded in the evaluation: this edge carries the paradigm, the GPT-3 edge carries the artifact; both channels are separately documented in the parent. Date and direction sound (2020 < 2022). Provisional, not verified, on the Q1 qualification.

react-2022.name: ReAct
react-2022.definition: Prompting framework (Yao et al., 2022) interleaving reasoning traces with environment actions; beat imitation/RL baselines by 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop.
react-2022.bottleneck: Before ReAct, a language model could reason or act but not interleave the two, because reasoning traces were disconnected from environment feedback.
react-2022.leap: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaved thought, action, and observation; with 1-2 exemplars it beat imitation/RL baselines by 34 points on ALFWorld and 10 on WebShop.
react-2022.prior_state: CoT reasoned blind (hallucination, error propagation); act-only policies could not plan or recover.

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (arXiv:2210.03629)

verification.notes: Multiples test partially lands: MRKL (May 2022) is a near-simultaneous alternative tool-use architecture, so necessity is 'ripe' rather than unique - but ReAct's reasoning-acting synergy result has no simultaneous equal. Q1 attack: RL/imitation agents already solved ALFWorld; ReAct's flip is specific to prompted LLMs. Date (Oct 2022) and causal direction check out. Mediation attack via CoT fails: CoT is a component inside ReAct, not a channel between ReAct and the agent.

transformer-architecture-2017.name: Transformer architecture
transformer-architecture-2017.definition: Sequence architecture based entirely on self-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017), replacing recurrence and enabling large-scale parallel training.
transformer-architecture-2017.bottleneck: Before the Transformer, sequence models could not train in parallel over long contexts, because recurrence forced sequential computation and vanishing information flow.
transformer-architecture-2017.leap: 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017) reached state-of-the-art translation in a fraction of prior training time and became the substrate of every frontier model that followed.
transformer-architecture-2017.prior_state: LSTM/GRU encoder-decoders with attention add-ons; slow sequential training and limited context.

sources.title: Why is ChatGPT so good? (Scale AI)
Attention Is All You Need

verification.notes: Verification for the GPT-1 edge specifically. Q1 attack fails: without self-attention GPT-1's parallelizable long-context training is a different, weaker system. Multiples test partially lands: by mid-2018 many labs were adopting the Transformer simultaneously, so necessity is 'ripe' at field level - but GPT-1's lineage necessity is specific (its model IS a Transformer decoder). Date/direction verified (Jun 2017 -> Jun 2018; GPT-1 paper states its architecture largely follows the original Transformer). Mediation attack via Bahdanau attention and via seq2seq both fail: those are the Transformer's own ancestors, not a channel between the Transformer and GPT-1 - GPT-1 consumed the architecture directly. This edge gives the Transformer in-degree 2 (agent + GPT-1): the run's second convergence. Node stays provisional.

large-scale-pretraining-gpt-3-2020.name: Large-scale pretraining (GPT-3)
large-scale-pretraining-gpt-3-2020.definition: Training very large autoregressive language models on web-scale text; GPT-3 (175B) showed few-shot in-context task performance without fine-tuning.
large-scale-pretraining-gpt-3-2020.bottleneck: Before GPT-3, a single model could not perform new tasks without gradient updates, because pretraining had never been scaled to the point where few-shot conditioning worked.
large-scale-pretraining-gpt-3-2020.leap: GPT-3 (175B, 2020) showed few-shot in-context task performance rivaling fine-tuned systems - one model, programmed by examples, replacing per-task training.
large-scale-pretraining-gpt-3-2020.prior_state: BERT-era practice: pretrain, then fine-tune a separate model per task.

reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedba.name: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedba.definition: Training recipe that fine-tunes a language model with a reward model learned from human preference rankings, aligning outputs with judged helpfulness.
reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedba.bottleneck: Before RLHF, deployed language models could not be steered to follow human intent reliably, because pretraining optimizes text completion, not judged helpfulness.
reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedba.leap: RLHF fine-tuning (InstructGPT, 2022) made a 1.3B model preferred over the 175B GPT-3 - a discontinuous jump in instruction-following at fixed scale.
reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedba.prior_state: LLMs could be prompted or demonstration-tuned, but outputs were often unhelpful, evasive, or toxic; no deployed model reliably followed open-ended instructions.

hosted-llm-apis-openai-api-2020.name: Hosted LLM APIs (OpenAI API)
hosted-llm-apis-openai-api-2020.definition: Commercial API access to GPT-3 (June 2020 beta) and successors; models as a metered cloud service.
hosted-llm-apis-openai-api-2020.bottleneck: Before hosted LLM APIs, using a frontier model required training or hosting it yourself, because no one sold metered access to a general model.
hosted-llm-apis-openai-api-2020.leap: The OpenAI API (June 2020) made GPT-3 a metered cloud service; by 2023 the agent ecosystem ran overwhelmingly on hosted frontier APIs.
hosted-llm-apis-openai-api-2020.prior_state: Downloadable checkpoints for small models; in-house serving for large ones.

chain-of-thought-prompting-2022.name: Chain-of-thought prompting
chain-of-thought-prompting-2022.definition: Prompting method (Wei et al., 2022) in which exemplars with intermediate reasoning steps elicit step-by-step reasoning; PaLM 540B with 8 exemplars set GSM8K state of the art.
chain-of-thought-prompting-2022.bottleneck: Before chain-of-thought, large models could not do multi-step reasoning in the open, because they had to answer in one forward leap from question to answer.
chain-of-thought-prompting-2022.leap: CoT prompting (Wei et al., 2022): 8 exemplars made PaLM 540B set GSM8K state of the art (58.1%), surpassing fine-tuned GPT-3 with a verifier - reasoning as an elicitable behavior.
chain-of-thought-prompting-2022.prior_state: Standard prompting gave flat scaling on reasoning tasks; scratchpad methods existed only as trained-from-scratch curiosities.

chatgpt-2022.name: ChatGPT
chatgpt-2022.definition: OpenAI's November 2022 product: an RLHF-tuned GPT-3.5 model in a chat interface; fastest-adopted consumer application of its time.
chatgpt-2022.bottleneck: Before ChatGPT, the public and builders could not interact with an aligned LLM as a general assistant, because aligned models existed only as research demos and APIs for specialists.
chatgpt-2022.leap: ChatGPT (Nov 30, 2022) put an RLHF-tuned model in a chat product reaching 100M users in two months - the fastest-adopted application to that date - and became the surface agent frameworks wrapped.
chatgpt-2022.prior_state: GPT-3 playground/API for developers; chatbots with narrow skills for consumers.

codex-code-generation-model-2021.name: Codex code generation model
codex-code-generation-model-2021.definition: GPT model fine-tuned on public code (OpenAI, 2021) powering Copilot; showed LLMs could produce working programs from natural language.
codex-code-generation-model-2021.bottleneck: Before Codex, a machine could not turn a natural-language specification into working code at useful reliability, because code models had never been trained at GPT scale on public repositories.
codex-code-generation-model-2021.leap: Codex (2021) solved 28.8% of HumanEval problems zero-shot (vs 0% for GPT-3), and powered Copilot - code as a general actuation channel for LLMs.
codex-code-generation-model-2021.prior_state: Program synthesis research systems and autocomplete over tokens, neither usable as a general tool.

instruction-tuning-flan-2021.name: Instruction tuning (FLAN)
instruction-tuning-flan-2021.definition: Fine-tuning language models on mixtures of tasks phrased as instructions, yielding zero-shot task following (FLAN, T0).
instruction-tuning-flan-2021.bottleneck: Before instruction tuning, language models could not perform unseen tasks from a plain-language specification, because they had only ever been trained to continue text.
instruction-tuning-flan-2021.leap: FLAN (2021) showed fine-tuning on 60+ instruction-phrased tasks yields large zero-shot gains on unseen tasks - task following as a trainable, general capability.
instruction-tuning-flan-2021.prior_state: Zero-shot task performance required per-task fine-tuning or careful few-shot prompt craft.

retrieval-augmented-generation-2020.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
retrieval-augmented-generation-2020.definition: Architecture coupling a parametric language model with a non-parametric retrieval index over external documents (Lewis et al., 2020).
retrieval-augmented-generation-2020.bottleneck: Before RAG, a language model's knowledge was frozen at training time, because generation had no channel to external, updatable memory.
retrieval-augmented-generation-2020.leap: RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) coupled a retriever to a generator and beat closed-book models on open-domain QA, establishing retrieval as a model component.
retrieval-augmented-generation-2020.prior_state: Closed-book LMs answering from weights; separate IR pipelines feeding rigid templates.

instructgpt-2022.name: InstructGPT
instructgpt-2022.definition: OpenAI's GPT-3 fine-tuned with supervised demonstrations plus RLHF; labelers preferred its outputs to a 100x larger base model.
instructgpt-2022.bottleneck: Before InstructGPT, no one had shown a language model could be made to follow instructions better by training on human judgments, because alignment had not been operationalized as a training pipeline.
instructgpt-2022.leap: InstructGPT (Mar 2022) was the first system whose smaller aligned model beat its 100x larger base model on human preference - the steering discontinuity, demonstrated.
instructgpt-2022.prior_state: GPT-3 deployments relied on prompt engineering; outputs frequently ignored the instruction's intent.

gpt-2-2019.name: GPT-2
gpt-2-2019.bottleneck: Before GPT-2, eliciting a new task from a model required training on that task, because no one had shown behavior could be specified by conditioning on text alone.
gpt-2-2019.leap: GPT-2 (2019) showed a pretrained language model performs tasks it was never trained on when the task is specified in the prompt text - zero-shot task transfer by conditioning, improving log-linearly with model size.
gpt-2-2019.prior_state: Per-task supervised training and fine-tuning; a model's abilities were fixed by its training run.

generative-pretraining-gpt-1-2018.name: Generative pretraining (GPT-1)
generative-pretraining-gpt-1-2018.definition: OpenAI model (Radford et al., 2018): a 117M Transformer decoder pretrained on BooksCorpus, then fine-tuned per task, beating purpose-built models on 9 of 12 language-understanding tasks.
generative-pretraining-gpt-1-2018.bottleneck: Before generative pretraining (GPT-1), transferring a language model to a new task required task-specific architectures and training, because no single pretrained model could be adapted by fine-tuning alone.
generative-pretraining-gpt-1-2018.leap: GPT-1 (2018) showed a Transformer decoder pretrained generatively on BooksCorpus, then fine-tuned, beats purpose-built models on 9 of 12 language-understanding tasks - founding the pretrain-then-adapt recipe GPT-2 scaled.
generative-pretraining-gpt-1-2018.prior_state: Task-specific architectures trained from scratch or from static word embeddings; transfer limited to word vectors.

byte-pair-encoding-for-nmt-2016.name: Byte-pair encoding for NMT
byte-pair-encoding-for-nmt-2016.definition: Segmentation method (Sennrich et al., 2016) applying byte-pair encoding to learn subword units, fixing rare-word handling in neural MT.
byte-pair-encoding-for-nmt-2016.bottleneck: Before byte-pair encoding for NMT, neural models were confined to fixed word vocabularies, because rare and unseen words could not be represented compositionally.
byte-pair-encoding-for-nmt-2016.leap: Sennrich et al. (2016) adapted BPE to segment rare words into frequent subword units, giving fixed-vocabulary open-vocabulary modeling (up to +1.1-1.3 BLEU) - the tokenizer scheme GPT-1 adopted with 40,000 merges.
byte-pair-encoding-for-nmt-2016.prior_state: Fixed vocabularies with unknown-word back-off dictionaries.

semi-supervised-sequence-learning-2015.name: Semi-supervised sequence learning
semi-supervised-sequence-learning-2015.definition: Method (Dai & Le, 2015) pretraining sequence models by LM/autoencoding before supervised fine-tuning, improving classification.
semi-supervised-sequence-learning-2015.bottleneck: Before semi-supervised sequence learning, sequence models had to be trained from random initialization on labeled data alone, because no recipe existed for initializing them from unlabeled text.
semi-supervised-sequence-learning-2015.leap: Dai & Le (2015) showed language-model and sequence-autoencoder pretraining stabilizes and improves supervised LSTM sequence learning - the first clear pretrain-then-fine-tune recipe for sequence models.
semi-supervised-sequence-learning-2015.prior_state: Supervised training from scratch; unlabeled text used at most to initialize word embeddings.

bookscorpus-2015.name: BooksCorpus
bookscorpus-2015.definition: Dataset (Zhu et al., 2015) of 11,038 unpublished books (~74M sentences) used to train the original GPT.
bookscorpus-2015.bottleneck: Before BooksCorpus, training language models on long contiguous narrative text was impractical because no large free corpus of complete books had been assembled.
bookscorpus-2015.leap: Zhu et al. (2015) assembled 11,038 free books (about 985M words) of long contiguous text, enabling unsupervised pretraining at book scale - the corpus GPT-1 was trained on.
bookscorpus-2015.prior_state: Sentence-shuffled news/web corpora such as One Billion Word, lacking long-range narrative structure.

common-crawl-2008.name: Common Crawl
common-crawl-2008.definition: Nonprofit web archive (founded 2007-08) providing petabytes of crawled web pages used to train many LMs.
common-crawl-2008.bottleneck: Before Common Crawl, training language models on web-scale text was impractical because no large, regularly refreshed crawl of the public web existed as an open corpus.
common-crawl-2008.leap: Common Crawl built a multi-billion-page open web archive - the raw resource GPT-3 filtered into 410 billion tokens, 60% of its weighted training mix.
common-crawl-2008.prior_state: Hand-assembled corpora (news, books, Wikipedia) orders of magnitude smaller than web scale.

sparse-transformer-2019.name: Sparse Transformer
sparse-transformer-2019.definition: Architecture (Child et al., 2019, OpenAI): factorized strided+local attention patterns reducing self-attention complexity for long sequences.
sparse-transformer-2019.bottleneck: Before the Sparse Transformer, self-attention cost grew quadratically with sequence length, because every position attended to every other position.
sparse-transformer-2019.leap: Child et al. (2019) factorized attention into strided and local patterns, making long-sequence Transformer training practical - GPT-3 adopted its alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention patterns.
sparse-transformer-2019.prior_state: Dense attention only; long contexts prohibitively expensive in compute and memory.

ppo-proximal-policy-optimization-2017.name: PPO (proximal policy optimization)
ppo-proximal-policy-optimization-2017.definition: Policy-gradient RL algorithm (Schulman et al., 2017) with clipped surrogate objective; the standard optimizer for RLHF.
ppo-proximal-policy-optimization-2017.bottleneck: Before PPO, policy-gradient updates were unstable and implementation-heavy, because trust-region methods required second-order machinery to avoid performance collapse.
ppo-proximal-policy-optimization-2017.leap: Schulman et al. (2017) introduced the clipped surrogate objective - trust-region-like stability from a simple first-order method; PPO became the optimizer used at every step of the RLHF lineage (Ziegler, Stiennon, InstructGPT).
ppo-proximal-policy-optimization-2017.prior_state: TRPO's constrained optimization and high-variance vanilla policy gradients.

deep-rl-from-human-preferences-christian.name: Deep RL from human preferences (Christiano et al.)
deep-rl-from-human-preferences-christian.definition: Method (Christiano et al., 2017) learning a reward model from human preferences over trajectory segments and optimizing it with RL.
deep-rl-from-human-preferences-christian.bottleneck: Before deep RL from human preferences, RL agents needed a hand-specified reward function, because human judgments about behavior could not be turned into a trainable objective.
deep-rl-from-human-preferences-christian.leap: Christiano et al. deep-rl-from-human-preferences-christian.prior_state: Hand-engineered reward functions; inverse RL requiring expert demonstrations.

learning-to-summarize-from-human-feedbac.leap: Stiennon et al. ran the full recipe (human comparisons, Bradley-Terry reward model, PPO with reference-KL penalty) on summarization: labelers preferred a 1.3B RLHF model over supervised models ten times its size and over the human reference summaries - the direct template InstructGPT copied.
learning-to-summarize-from-human-feedbac.prior_state: Ziegler-scale demonstrations whose summarizers exploited labeler heuristics by copying source sentences.

fine-tuning-language-models-from-human-p.name: Fine-tuning language models from human preferences (Ziegler et al.)
fine-tuning-language-models-from-human-p.definition: Method (Ziegler et al., 2019, OpenAI): train a reward model from human comparisons and fine-tune a pretrained LM (GPT-2) with PPO under a KL penalty.
fine-tuning-language-models-from-human-p.bottleneck: Before Ziegler et al. (2019), reward learning from human preferences had only been shown in simulated control tasks, because no one had applied it to real language problems.
fine-tuning-language-models-from-human-p.leap: Ziegler et al. applied reward modeling plus PPO with a KL penalty to GPT-2, steering text style and summarization from as few as 5,000 human comparisons - the first RLHF for language models.
fine-tuning-language-models-from-human-p.prior_state: Programmatic rewards (BLEU/ROUGE) as poor proxies for human judgment in language RL.

Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences

verification.notes: Verdict: provisional. Direct scale predecessor; Q3 held at partial by the Boehm/Jaques multiples.

trpo-trust-region-policy-optimization-20.name: TRPO (trust region policy optimization)
trpo-trust-region-policy-optimization-20.definition: Algorithm (Schulman et al., 2015): policy updates constrained to a trust region via a KL bound, with monotonic-improvement guarantees.
trpo-trust-region-policy-optimization-20.bottleneck: Before TRPO, policy updates had no practical stability guarantee, because a single oversized gradient step could collapse a learned policy irreversibly.
trpo-trust-region-policy-optimization-20.leap: Schulman et al. (2015) constrained each update to a KL trust region and proved monotonic improvement, making large policy-gradient updates safe in practice - the guarantee PPO later approximated with clipping.
trpo-trust-region-policy-optimization-20.prior_state: Vanilla policy gradients with hand-tuned step sizes; natural-gradient theory without a practical deep-RL algorithm.

verification.notes: Mediation attack via natural policy gradient fails: TRPO is the paper that turned trust-region theory into a practical deep-RL algorithm, and it is the artifact PPO explicitly simplifies (same lead author). Multiples: DDPG and other 2015-16 algorithms coexisted, but the trust-region line is the consumed one. Verdict: provisional.

reinforce-williams-1992.name: REINFORCE (Williams)
reinforce-williams-1992.definition: Algorithm (Williams, 1992): gradient ascent on expected reward using sampled returns - the original policy-gradient estimator.
reinforce-williams-1992.bottleneck: Before REINFORCE, connectionist systems could not learn from scalar evaluative feedback, because no gradient estimator existed for expected reward.
reinforce-williams-1992.leap: Williams (1992) derived the likelihood-ratio gradient estimator for expected reward - the founding algorithm of the policy-gradient family that TRPO and PPO descend from.
reinforce-williams-1992.prior_state: Supervised learning from labeled targets; bandit heuristics without gradient foundations.

verification.notes: Q1 attack: REINFORCE's variance made it impractical at scale - true, and priced into Q4/Q9 fails; the impossibility flip (learning from scalar evaluative feedback by gradient ascent) stands as the family's founding move. No multiples in 1992 for this estimator class. Verdict: provisional.

generalized-advantage-estimation-gae-201.name: Generalized advantage estimation (GAE)
generalized-advantage-estimation-gae-201.definition: Estimator (Schulman et al., 2016): exponentially-weighted advantage estimates trading bias against variance via a lambda parameter.
generalized-advantage-estimation-gae-201.bottleneck: Before GAE, advantage estimates forced a crude choice between high bias (one-step TD) and high variance (full returns), destabilizing policy-gradient training.
generalized-advantage-estimation-gae-201.leap: Schulman et al. (2016) introduced the lambda-weighted advantage estimator that smoothly trades bias against variance - the advantage signal consumed by TRPO/PPO implementations and, later, every RLHF codebase.
generalized-advantage-estimation-gae-201.prior_state: Fixed-horizon returns and one-step temporal-difference advantages.

verification.notes: GAE initially missed the (Q1 OR Q2) gate with both graded partial; on re-examination of the primary source, Q2 was corrected to pass before the single clean application of verdicts: the paper's demonstrated effect was policy optimization on high-dimensional continuous control (3D locomotion) previously impractical, i.e. a generativity flip for the family, and PPO's objective is defined over GAE advantages in standard practice. Mediation attack via TRPO fails: estimator and optimizer are distinct contributions, published separately, consumed together. Verdict: provisional.

policy-gradient-theorem-sutton-et-al-200.name: Policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al.)
policy-gradient-theorem-sutton-et-al-200.definition: Theorem (Sutton, McAllester, Singh & Mansour, 2000): the gradient of expected return can be written without differentiating the state distribution.
policy-gradient-theorem-sutton-et-al-200.bottleneck: Before the policy gradient theorem, differentiating expected return looked intractable, because the state distribution itself depends on the policy.
policy-gradient-theorem-sutton-et-al-200.leap: Sutton, McAllester, Singh & Mansour (2000) proved the policy gradient needs no derivative of the state distribution - the mathematical license for the entire policy-gradient family, PPO included.
policy-gradient-theorem-sutton-et-al-200.prior_state: REINFORCE-style estimators used without a general function-approximation theory.

bahdanau-attention-2014.name: Bahdanau attention
bahdanau-attention-2014.definition: Mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2014) letting a decoder attend over encoder states in neural MT.
bahdanau-attention-2014.bottleneck: Before Bahdanau attention, seq2seq compressed an entire source sentence into one fixed-length vector, because the decoder had no way to look back at individual source positions.
bahdanau-attention-2014.leap: Bahdanau et al. (2014) let the decoder attend over all encoder states at each decoding step - quality stopped collapsing on long sentences, and attention became a reusable mechanism separable from recurrence.

sources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

verification.notes: Multiples attack partially lands: Luong et al. (2015) published alternative attention forms within a year and Parikh et al. (2016) showed attention-only models for NLI - the idea was ripe; necessity graded partial. But Bahdanau et al. is the cited origin of the mechanism the Transformer generalizes, and the mediation attack via seq2seq fails (attention is precisely the addition seq2seq lacked). Verdict: provisional.

sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014.name: Sequence-to-sequence learning
sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014.definition: Framework (Sutskever et al., 2014) mapping sequences to sequences with LSTM encoder-decoders.
sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014.bottleneck: Before seq2seq, sequence transduction needed task-specific architectures and hand-built alignments, because no single learned model mapped variable-length inputs to variable-length outputs.
sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014.leap: Sutskever et al. (2014) showed one LSTM encoder-decoder trained end to end could reach near-state-of-the-art translation - the template, task framing, and substrate that attention and then the Transformer were built on.
sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014.prior_state: Phrase-based statistical MT pipelines and fixed-length neural encoders.

sources.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

verification.notes: Multiples/precursor note: Kalchbrenner & Blunsom (2013) had a recurrent encoder-decoder for translation a year earlier; Sutskever et al. is the canonical consumed artifact (deep LSTMs, end-to-end, near-SOTA) that defined the template. Mediation attack via LSTM fails: the encoder-decoder framing, not the cell, is the contribution. Verdict: provisional.

bradley-terry-model-of-paired-comparison.name: Bradley-Terry model of paired comparisons
bradley-terry-model-of-paired-comparison.definition: Statistical model (Bradley & Terry, 1952): probability that one item beats another is a logistic function of latent scores.
bradley-terry-model-of-paired-comparison.bottleneck: Before Bradley-Terry, paired human judgments had no probabilistic model, because there was no principled way to turn 'A beats B' outcomes into latent scores.
bradley-terry-model-of-paired-comparison.leap: Bradley & Terry (1952) modeled pairwise wins as a logistic function of latent item scores - the exact functional form Christiano et al.'s reward model (and every RLHF reward model after) fits to human comparisons.
bradley-terry-model-of-paired-comparison.prior_state: Thurstone's law of comparative judgment (1927) as the main alternative formulation.

sources.title: Bradley-Terry model

verification.notes: Verdict: provisional. Time-floor node (1952) gains a third consumer edge (after Christiano via RLHF expansion and now Stiennon).

inverse-reinforcement-learning-ng-russel.name: Inverse reinforcement learning (Ng & Russell)
inverse-reinforcement-learning-ng-russel.definition: Framework (Ng & Russell, 2000): recover a reward function from an expert's observed behavior.
inverse-reinforcement-learning-ng-russel.bottleneck: Before inverse RL, the only way to specify what an agent should do was to hand-write a reward function, because behavior itself carried no recoverable objective.
inverse-reinforcement-learning-ng-russel.leap: Ng & Russell (2000) formalized recovering a reward function from an expert's behavior - establishing 'learn the reward, then optimize it' as a research program, the program Christiano et al. re-aimed from demonstrations to preferences.
inverse-reinforcement-learning-ng-russel.prior_state: Hand-engineered reward functions as the sole specification channel.

verification.notes: Q1 attack partially lands: IRL's expert demonstrations are often unavailable - which is precisely the limitation Christiano et al. cite as motivation; the flip IRL itself made (reward as recoverable object) stands. Mediation attack via apprenticeship learning fails on direction (apprenticeship learning is IRL's descendant, not its mediator). Verdict: provisional.

tamer-framework-knox-stone-2009.name: TAMER framework (Knox & Stone)
tamer-framework-knox-stone-2009.definition: Framework (Knox & Stone, 2009): agents learn from human evaluative feedback (+/-) treated as reward.
tamer-framework-knox-stone-2009.bottleneck: Before TAMER, human feedback during training was anecdotal, because no framework treated a trainer's evaluative signals as a learnable reward channel.
tamer-framework-knox-stone-2009.leap: Knox & Stone (2009) showed agents can learn from human +/- feedback modeled as reward - the first systematic human-in-the-loop RL channel, the direct conceptual predecessor of preference-based feedback.
tamer-framework-knox-stone-2009.prior_state: Fully autonomous RL from environment rewards only.

verification.notes: Signal-type caveat recorded: TAMER's feedback is evaluative (+/-) rather than comparative; Christiano et al.'s comparisons are its scalable successor, not a copy - the edge records the human-feedback channel's origin. Multiples: COACH (2017) is coeval with Christiano, not with TAMER. Verdict: provisional.

bidirectional-recurrent-neural-networks-.name: Bidirectional recurrent neural networks
bidirectional-recurrent-neural-networks-.definition: Architecture (Schuster & Paliwal, IEEE Trans. Signal Processing 1997): two recurrent layers processing a sequence in opposite directions so each position's representation summarizes both past and future context.
bidirectional-recurrent-neural-networks-.bottleneck: Before bidirectional RNNs, a recurrent encoder's representation of each position could only summarize what came before it, because the recurrence ran in one direction only.
bidirectional-recurrent-neural-networks-.leap: Schuster & Paliwal (1997) ran recurrence in both directions and concatenated the states, so every position's representation summarizes its whole surrounding context - the annotation format attention later learned to search over.
bidirectional-recurrent-neural-networks-.prior_state: Recurrent sequence encoders were unidirectional; position representations carried no future context.

sources.title: Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks

verification.notes: Verdict: provisional. Notable: this node gives the attention lineage a 1997 trunk on the encoder side, complementing the 2013 mechanism-side survivor.

generating-sequences-with-recurrent-neur.name: Generating sequences with recurrent neural networks (Graves soft window)
generating-sequences-with-recurrent-neur.definition: Model and mechanism (Graves, 2013): deep LSTM sequence generation whose handwriting-synthesis network conditions on a text through a differentiable soft window (mixture of Gaussians) that learns the alignment between characters and pen strokes.
generating-sequences-with-recurrent-neur.bottleneck: Before Graves' soft window, a neural sequence generator could not look back at a specific part of its input while generating, because no differentiable mechanism existed for a network to learn an alignment between input positions and output steps.
generating-sequences-with-recurrent-neur.leap: Graves (2013) gave an LSTM generator a differentiable soft window over its input - a Gaussian mixture the network slides forward as it writes - so input-output alignment became a learned, end-to-end quantity rather than a pre-segmented given.
generating-sequences-with-recurrent-neur.prior_state: Sequence generation conditioned on an annotation sequence required pre-segmented alignments (CTC-style or HMM pipelines) or no alignment at all.

sources.title: Generating Sequences With Recurrent Neural Networks

verification.notes: Verdict: provisional. The strongest survivor of this expansion: the only candidate with a named, mechanism-level citation channel into the parent paper.

long-short-term-memory-lstm-1997.name: Long short-term memory (LSTM)
long-short-term-memory-lstm-1997.definition: Gated recurrent unit (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) whose constant error carousel carries information and gradients across long time lags without vanishing.
long-short-term-memory-lstm-1997.bottleneck: Before LSTM, learning long-range dependencies in recurrent networks was impossible in practice because gradients vanished or exploded across long time lags.
long-short-term-memory-lstm-1997.leap: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997) showed a gated memory cell with a constant error carousel could learn dependencies over very long lags that gradient descent on plain RNNs provably could not.
long-short-term-memory-lstm-1997.prior_state: Plain RNNs trained by backpropagation through time, with the vanishing/exploding gradient problem formally characterized (Hochreiter 1991; Bengio et al. 1994) and no trainable long-memory cell.

sources.title: Long short-term memory (Wikipedia)
Generating Sequences With Recurrent Neural Networks (Graves, 2013)

(2) Multiples test: no simultaneous independent co-inventor of the gated CEC cell in the 1990s; the design is Hochreiter & Schmidhuber's singular contribution. (3) Date 1997 and causal direction (cell consumed verbatim in the paper's Sec. 2.1 equations) check out. (4) Mediation attack: the strongest candidate M is the modern cell form (forget gate 2000 + peepholes 2002) sitting between the 1997 paper and Graves' equations - but those variants were evaluated in this same expansion and gate-rejected as components of the LSTM leap; the 1997 core (CEC plus input/output gating) is directly consumed, so the mediation is not complete and the edge stands. Provisional on the Q1/necessity attack.

recurrent-neural-network-language-model-.name: Recurrent neural network language model (Mikolov)
recurrent-neural-network-language-model-.definition: A recurrent network trained to predict the next word from the previous words (Mikolov et al., 2010), which made variable-length conditional text generation a trainable objective.
recurrent-neural-network-language-model-.bottleneck: Before the RNN language model, neural language modeling used fixed-length contexts, because no trainable neural model predicted the next word from an unbounded history.
recurrent-neural-network-language-model-.leap: Mikolov et al. (2010) showed a simple recurrent network beats n-gram and feedforward models at language modeling, making next-word prediction from unbounded history a trainable, scalable objective.
recurrent-neural-network-language-model-.prior_state: Feedforward neural probabilistic language models with fixed context windows, and smoothed n-gram models.

sources.title: Generating Text with Recurrent Neural Networks (Sutskever et al. 2011)

verification.notes: Q1 attack: RNNLM flipped no impossibility (n-grams predicted next words), consistent with Q1=partial as evaluated. Multiples test on Q3: feedforward conditional LMs (Devlin-style joint models) were a live alternative in the abstract, but for this parent the paper's decoder is explicitly defined as an RNNLM conditioned on the input, citing the Mikolov line - necessity holds for the artifact as built, not as the only conceivable path. Date check: 2010 Interspeech paper, defensible. Mediation attack on RNNLM->seq2seq: candidate mediators Mikolov & Zweig context-RNNLM (2012) and Auli et al. (2013) carried conditioning for rescoring with topic/source features, a different conditioning source than the encoder state; the direct channel (the decoder's entire form is an RNNLM) dominates, so the attack does not land - no mediation object. Outcome provisional.

elman-recurrent-network-1990.name: Elman recurrent network
elman-recurrent-network-1990.definition: Simple recurrent network (Elman, 1990) with context units copying the hidden state, the standard RNN design BRNN extends.
elman-recurrent-network-1990.bottleneck: Before the Elman network, feedforward models had no mechanism for sequence context, because no trainable state summarized the past.
elman-recurrent-network-1990.leap: Elman (1990) showed a simple recurrent network's hidden state learns to encode sequential structure - the base architecture the bidirectional design doubles.
elman-recurrent-network-1990.prior_state: Fixed-window feedforward models and hand-built temporal features.

Weakest-evidence attack on Q1: the identity of architecture is structural (one recurrent hidden layer, state fed back, next-item training objective), visible in both papers' model descriptions, not a name resemblance. Mediation attack: via backpropagation through time (the training procedure) - fails: a procedure cannot mediate the architecture it trains; BPTT is disposed at this parent as a component (leap-gate), and the architecture would be the parent's design under any trainer. iam-ondb-online-handwriting-database-200.name: IAM-OnDB online handwriting database
iam-ondb-online-handwriting-database-200.definition: Liwicki & Bunke's ICDAR 2005 database of unconstrained online handwriting acquired on a whiteboard, with transcriptions.
iam-ondb-online-handwriting-database-200.bottleneck: Before IAM-OnDB, no public corpus of unconstrained online handwriting sentences with transcriptions existed, so data-driven handwriting research at sentence level was impractical.
iam-ondb-online-handwriting-database-200.leap: IAM-OnDB released whiteboard-acquired pen traces with transcriptions from 221 writers, unblocking the online-handwriting research line from recognition (2007/2009) to generation (2013).
iam-ondb-online-handwriting-database-200.prior_state: Private or character-level handwriting collections without sentence transcriptions.

mixture-density-networks-bishop-1994.name: Mixture density networks (Bishop)
mixture-density-networks-bishop-1994.definition: Bishop's scheme (1994) in which a neural network outputs the weights, means and variances of a mixture distribution instead of a point prediction.
mixture-density-networks-bishop-1994.bottleneck: Before mixture density networks, a neural network could only predict a single point estimate, so multimodal real-valued targets were unrepresentable.
mixture-density-networks-bishop-1994.leap: Bishop's MDN made a network output the full parameters of a mixture distribution, turning regression into trainable density modelling.
mixture-density-networks-bishop-1994.prior_state: Least-squares regression networks that averaged mutually exclusive outcomes into a single mean prediction.

sources.title: Mixture Density Networks (Bishop, 1994)

(2) Multiples test lands partially: Bridle (1990) and Jacobs et al. (1991) are near-simultaneous ancestors of the mixture-output idea, so necessity is 'ripe' rather than singular - Bishop 1994 remains the canonical formulation the paper cites. hochreiter-s-1991-diploma-thesis-analysi.name: Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis analysis of vanishing and exploding gradients (Untersuchungen zu dynamischen neuronalen Netzen)
hochreiter-s-1991-diploma-thesis-analysi.bottleneck: Before LSTM, learning long-range dependencies in recurrent networks was impossible in practice because gradients vanished or exploded across long time lags.
hochreiter-s-1991-diploma-thesis-analysi.leap: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber (1997) showed a gated memory cell with a constant error carousel could learn dependencies over very long lags that gradient descent on plain RNNs provably could not.
hochreiter-s-1991-diploma-thesis-analysi.prior_state: Plain RNNs trained by backpropagation through time, with the vanishing/exploding gradient problem formally characterized (Hochreiter 1991; Bengio et al. 1994) and no trainable long-memory cell.

(2) Q1 attack - an analysis is not a leap: rebutted by graph precedent (Bradley-Terry model and the policy gradient theorem are nodes in this same graph); a formal result that converts an unexplained failure into a designable specification passes Q1, and this thesis additionally contained the first constant-error construction. (3) Mediation attack - the analysis is OF BPTT, not mediated by it: the 1997 paper Sec. 3 cites and re-derives the thesis directly; no intermediate work sits on the channel. tl-dr-dataset-webis-tldr-17-corpus-volsk.name: TL;DR dataset (Webis-TLDR-17 corpus) (Völske et al.)
tl-dr-dataset-webis-tldr-17-corpus-volsk.definition: Corpus (Völske et al., 2017): ~4M Reddit posts with author-written TL;DR summaries, mined from social media as a large abstractive summarization dataset.
tl-dr-dataset-webis-tldr-17-corpus-volsk.bottleneck: Before the Webis-TLDR-17 corpus, training a summarizer on subjective, author-written summaries at scale was impractical because existing corpora were news-wire (CNN/DM, Gigaword) whose quality signal is dominated by extractive overlap.
tl-dr-dataset-webis-tldr-17-corpus-volsk.leap: Corpus (Völske et al., 2017): ~4M Reddit posts with author-written TL;DR summaries, mined from social media as a large abstractive summarization dataset.
tl-dr-dataset-webis-tldr-17-corpus-volsk.prior_state: CNN/Daily Mail and Gigaword as the only large summarization corpora, both news genre; DUC corpora of a few hundred documents.

json-schema-2010.name: JSON Schema
json-schema-2010.definition: The IETF-drafted vocabulary (Zyp et al., from 2009-10) for annotating and validating JSON documents - the format in which LLM function-calling tool parameters are specified.
json-schema-2010.bottleneck: Before JSON Schema, the structure of data a program expects could not be declared and machine-validated in a standard way, because interface contracts lived in prose documentation.
json-schema-2010.leap: JSON Schema (IETF drafts from 2009-10, Zyp et al.) gave JSON a universal annotation and validation vocabulary - later embedded in OpenAPI and adopted wholesale as the parameter language of LLM function calling.
json-schema-2010.prior_state: Per-system conventions and prose API docs; validation hand-coded per consumer.

nvidia-v100-gpu-2017.definition: NVIDIA's Volta-generation data-center GPU (2017), the first with tensor cores and HBM2, built for mixed-precision deep learning at cluster scale.
nvidia-v100-gpu-2017.bottleneck: Before the V100, training a model at hundred-billion-parameter scale was impractical, because no accelerator combined tensor-core mixed-precision arithmetic with the memory bandwidth to feed it.
nvidia-v100-gpu-2017.leap: The V100 (Volta, 2017) introduced tensor cores and HBM2 in a data-center GPU, making mixed-precision training at cluster scale the default recipe of the scaling era.
nvidia-v100-gpu-2017.prior_state: P100-generation accelerators: no tensor cores, lower bandwidth; frontier runs were smaller and slower.

nvidia-tesla-p100-gpu-2016.name: NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU
nvidia-tesla-p100-gpu-2016.definition: NVIDIA's Pascal-generation datacenter GPU (announced GTC, April 2016): first accelerator with HBM2 memory (720 GB/s) and NVLink interconnect (160 GB/s bidirectional); the training hardware documented in the Transformer paper (section 5.2: one machine with 8 P100s).
nvidia-tesla-p100-gpu-2016.bottleneck: Before Pascal-class accelerators, training a competitive sequence model meant weeks on large clusters; architecture iteration was gated by compute queues.
nvidia-tesla-p100-gpu-2016.leap: First datacenter GPU with HBM2 and NVLink, making the single-node 8-GPU training machine practical.
nvidia-tesla-p100-gpu-2016.prior_state: Kepler/Maxwell-era GPUs (K80/M40) with GDDR5 bandwidth and PCIe-only interconnect.

(1) Q1 attack: the edge claims no flip by P100 for V100 - the admission basis is ancestor-modified mechanism retention, documented section by section in the whitepaper (UM access counters over Pascal's page migration; MPS clients 16 -> 48; 'the same SECDED ECC protection ... in Pascal GP100'; 'maintains the same SXM2 board form factor as Tesla P100'); the attack does not reach it. (2) Multiples test on Q3: the carried mechanisms (UM, MPS, ECC scheme, FP16 datapath) are single-vendor internal designs with no independent multiple; necessity stays partial only because a clean-sheet design is conceivable in the abstract. (3) Date/direction: GP100 Apr 2016 precedes GV100 May 2017; direction is the whitepaper's own ('builds upon the advances of its predecessor, the Pascal GP100 GPU'). (4) Mediation attack - the strongest: via the separately-filed components (NVLink, HBM2, CoWoS), i.e. is the product-level edge redundant? It fails: the components are GP100's constituents, and the P100 edge carries a distinct stratum none of them carries - the unified-memory/page-migration design, MPS, the ECC scheme, the board form and the FP16 datapath lineage. The run's own practice admits distinct edges for distinct mechanism families at one parent (the Fisher trio at the treatise). Edge stands, provisional.

wmt-2014-english-german-parallel-corpus-.name: WMT 2014 English-German parallel corpus
wmt-2014-english-german-parallel-corpus-.definition: The standard WMT 2014 English-German training set of about 4.5 million sentence pairs (Europarl, News Commentary, Common Crawl components), as used in the Transformer paper's section 5.1.
wmt-2014-english-german-parallel-corpus-.bottleneck: Before a shared large parallel corpus existed, MT results were incomparable across labs and training data was a private advantage; the field had no common evidence base.
wmt-2014-english-german-parallel-corpus-.leap: Assembly and release of the ~4.5M-pair English-German training set as the shared task corpus of WMT 2014.
wmt-2014-english-german-parallel-corpus-.prior_state: Fragmented, partly proprietary parallel corpora; results reported on incompatible data.

google-brain-2011.name: Google Brain
google-brain-2011.definition: Google's large-scale deep learning research organization, founded in 2011 by Andrew Ng, Jeff Dean and Greg Corrado; institutional home of DistBelief, sequence-to-sequence learning's authors, the GNMT production program, and the Transformer paper's authors.
google-brain-2011.bottleneck: Before Google Brain (2011), no organization combined very large compute fleets, production ML surfaces, and a mandate for open-ended deep-learning research inside one team.
google-brain-2011.leap: Founding of Google's large-scale deep learning organization (2011): the institutional vehicle of the distributed-DL era.
google-brain-2011.prior_state: Academic labs and small industry groups training single-machine models.

openai-2015.name: OpenAI
openai-2015.definition: The research organization founded in 2015 (restructured with a capped-profit LP in 2019) whose alignment team produced the RLHF lineage: Christiano 2017, Ziegler 2019, Stiennon 2020, InstructGPT 2022.
openai-2015.bottleneck: Before OpenAI (2015), no organization combined frontier-scale LM development, a dedicated alignment program, and a deployed API product whose traffic could supply real instruction data.
openai-2015.leap: Founding of OpenAI (2015): the institutional vehicle that carried alignment research from preference learning to a deployed, instruction-following product.
openai-2015.prior_state: Academic alignment theory and lab-scale RL, with no deployed LM product in the loop.

realtoxicityprompts-gehman-et-al-2020.name: RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al.)
realtoxicityprompts-gehman-et-al-2020.definition: Gehman, Gururangan, Sap, Choi & Smith's EMNLP 2020 Findings testbed: 100K naturally occurring prompts showing pretrained LMs degenerate into toxic text even from innocuous prompts; the standard instrument on which InstructGPT reports its toxicity results.
realtoxicityprompts-gehman-et-al-2020.bottleneck: Before RealToxicityPrompts (2020), LM toxicity was anecdote: no shared, naturally occurring prompt set existed on which degeneration could be measured and compared.
realtoxicityprompts-gehman-et-al-2020.leap: Release of a 100K-prompt naturalistic testbed that made neural toxic degeneration a measurable, comparable quantity.
realtoxicityprompts-gehman-et-al-2020.prior_state: Ad-hoc prompt lists and classifier scores on synthetic examples; no common instrument.

cuda-gpu-computing-2007.name: CUDA GPU computing
cuda-gpu-computing-2007.definition: Software platform (NVIDIA, 2007): the parallel programming model and runtime that made NVIDIA GPUs programmable for general-purpose computation - the layer every deep-learning training stack of the 2010s executed on.
cuda-gpu-computing-2007.bottleneck: Before CUDA, general-purpose computation on GPUs was impractical because programming them meant disguising computation as graphics rendering in shader languages, so the parallel hardware sat unusable for general algorithms.
cuda-gpu-computing-2007.leap: CUDA (2007) made the GPU a general-purpose parallel computer: a C-based programming model of threads, blocks and shared memory turned graphics chips into programmable accelerators, and a decade later into the default training substrate of the deep-learning era.
cuda-gpu-computing-2007.prior_state: GPGPU via graphics APIs and shader tricks (Cg, GLSL, BrookGPU): computation expressed as rendering, with crippled memory access and control flow.

openapi-specification-2016.name: OpenAPI specification
openapi-specification-2016.definition: Specification (OpenAPI Initiative, standardized from Swagger 2014-2017): the standard machine-readable format for describing REST APIs - paths, operations, parameters, response schemas - consumed by tooling and, in 2023, by LLM agents to call third-party APIs.
openapi-specification-2016.bottleneck: Before the OpenAPI specification, what a third-party API could do existed only as human-readable documentation, because there was no standard machine-readable contract for paths, parameters and responses that a program - or an agent - could consume directly.
openapi-specification-2016.leap: The OpenAPI specification (standardized from Swagger, 2015-17) made REST APIs machine-describable in one universal format; a decade later it became a contract LLM agents consumed to turn existing web services into callable tools (ChatGPT plugins, 2023; GPT Actions after them).
openapi-specification-2016.prior_state: Per-provider prose documentation, WSDL-era formality for SOAP services, and a hand-written client wrapper for every integration.

nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-g80-2006.name: NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTX (G80)
aliases: NVIDIA G80 unified graphics and compute architecture
NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTX (G80) unified shader architecture
Tesla unified graphics and computing architecture (G80 generation)
nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-g80-2006.definition: Launched 8 November 2006, the first CUDA-capable graphics card: G80 architecture, 128 unified stream processors, 768 MB GDDR3 on a 384-bit bus.
nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-g80-2006.bottleneck: Before the GeForce 8800 GTX (G80), a massively parallel processor that a general C program could address was impractical because GPUs split fixed vertex and pixel pipelines with gather-only memory access.
nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-g80-2006.leap: The G80 (Nov 2006) unified 128 scalar stream processors with shared memory and global load/store, the first shipping silicon a general-purpose parallel programming model could target.
nvidia-geforce-8800-gtx-g80-2006.prior_state: Split vertex/pixel pipelines (GeForce 7 series), gather-only fragment programming, and rival throughput designs locked in consoles (Xenos) or exotic programming models (Cell).

brookgpu-stream-and-kernel-abstraction-2.name: BrookGPU stream and kernel abstraction

BrookGPU compiler limited by graphics APIs
brookgpu-stream-and-kernel-abstraction-2.definition: Stanford's Brook extension to C treating data as streams and functions as kernels, compiled to GPUs via graphics APIs from 2004.
brookgpu-stream-and-kernel-abstraction-2.bottleneck: Before BrookGPU, using a GPU as a data-parallel coprocessor was impractical because programs had to be hand-disguised as graphics rendering in shader languages.
brookgpu-stream-and-kernel-abstraction-2.leap: BrookGPU (2004) recast the GPU as a streaming coprocessor programmable in extended C — streams, kernels and reductions — the model CUDA's author carried into NVIDIA and rebuilt natively.
brookgpu-stream-and-kernel-abstraction-2.prior_state: Hand-written Cg/GLSL shader GPGPU: arrays as textures, computation as fragment passes, gather-only memory access.

json-rfc-4627-2006.name: JSON (RFC 4627)
json-rfc-4627-2006.definition: Crockford's 2006 RFC formalizing JSON as a lightweight text format for structured data derived from ECMAScript, providing the instance model JSON Schema describes.
json-rfc-4627-2006.bottleneck: Before JSON (RFC 4627), structured data interchange on the web had no lightweight, language-independent text format with a fixed data model, because the incumbent was XML with its document (not data) model and heavyweight parsing.
json-rfc-4627-2006.leap: Crockford's extraction of the JavaScript object-literal subset (from 2001), formalized as RFC 4627 in July 2006, fixed a six-type data model - objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null - that became the web's default data format and the instance model every later JSON vocabulary annotates.
json-rfc-4627-2006.prior_state: Web data interchange meant XML documents with schemas and parsers built for documents, or ad hoc per-language serialization formats.

(2) Multiples on Q3: YAML (2001) is a near-simultaneous rival for the same role and XML remained viable - necessity is ripe/substitutable, so the node may not be verified on necessity grounds; capped at provisional. (4) Mediation attack: ECMAScript named as candidate M fails - JSON was extracted FROM the literals, and the schema consumes the extracted format directly; extraction is the opposite direction from mediation. No mediation object. Outcome: provisional.

w3c-xml-schema-xsd-2001.name: W3C XML Schema (XSD)
w3c-xml-schema-xsd-2001.definition: The W3C's 2001 Recommendation for declaring XML structure and datatypes, the principal ancestor whose declarative validation model JSON Schema ported to JSON.
w3c-xml-schema-xsd-2001.bottleneck: Before W3C XML Schema, declaring the structure and datatypes of a document in a standard, machine-checkable vocabulary was impossible because DTDs had no datatype system and no namespace awareness.
w3c-xml-schema-xsd-2001.leap: The 2001 W3C Recommendation supplied the schema-language model - named types, a datatype hierarchy with constraining facets (length, pattern, minimum, maximum, enumeration), and occurrence/structure declarations written in the format's own syntax - the model later schema languages, JSON Schema included, transposed to their formats.
w3c-xml-schema-xsd-2001.prior_state: DTD grammar declarations without datatypes; per-vendor schema dialects (XML-Data, XDR, SOX) competing without a standard.

No mediation object. Outcome: provisional.

json-referencing-in-dojo-2008.name: JSON Referencing in Dojo
json-referencing-in-dojo-2008.definition: The SitePen/Dojo JSON Referencing convention of 2008 using $ref values to link JSON objects, later carried into JSON Schema's referencing mechanism.
json-referencing-in-dojo-2008.bottleneck: Before JSON Referencing, JSON documents could not point at one another's values with a standard convention, because references were hand-managed identifiers with per-system resolution rules.
json-referencing-in-dojo-2008.leap: Zyp and the SitePen/Dojo community's 2008 JSON Referencing convention - $ref values linking JSON objects across documents - gave JSON a standard cross-reference mechanism, carried by its author into JSON Schema, where $ref became the schema-reuse and composition mechanism.
json-referencing-in-dojo-2008.prior_state: Per-system identifier conventions; schemas and object graphs duplicated shared structure inline because no reference convention existed.

(2) Multiples on Q3: named-type reuse existed in XSD and RELAX NG for their own formats - the JSON-native path was ripe, not unique in principle; capped at provisional. kris-zyp-s-first-json-schema-proposal-js.name: Kris Zyp's first JSON Schema proposal (json.com)
kris-zyp-s-first-json-schema-proposal-js.definition: Zyp's 2007 proposal submitted to json.com, the origin point the JSON Schema project itself dates its history to, preceding draft-zyp-json-schema-00 of December 2009.
kris-zyp-s-first-json-schema-proposal-js.bottleneck: Before Zyp's 2007 proposal, the task of describing and validating JSON structure in JSON itself had never been formulated as a named problem, because schema thinking was bound to XML documents.
kris-zyp-s-first-json-schema-proposal-js.leap: On 2 October 2007 Zyp submitted to json.com the first JSON Schema proposal: a vocabulary, written in JSON, for describing and validating JSON structure - the formulation the JSON Schema project itself dates its history to, and the direct ancestor text of the 2009-10 IETF drafts by the same author.
kris-zyp-s-first-json-schema-proposal-js.prior_state: JSON validation existed only as hand-coded checks or as XML-schema thinking applied to a non-XML format; Kwalify validated YAML/JSON data in its own idiom without posing the JSON-native vocabulary task.

the-json-org-one-page-grammar-2002.name: The json.org one-page grammar
the-json-org-one-page-grammar-2002.definition: Crockford's 2002 single-page publication of the JSON grammar at json.org, the format's only specification until the RFC.
the-json-org-one-page-grammar-2002.bottleneck: Before the json.org one-page grammar, JavaScript literals could not function as a public data format, because the notation had no name, no published grammar, and no license outside one company.
the-json-org-one-page-grammar-2002.leap: Crockford published the entire format on one page (2002) - five railroad diagrams and a permissive license - turning a company-internal trick into a specification anyone could implement in an afternoon.
the-json-org-one-page-grammar-2002.prior_state: The literal-as-data trick existed as folklore inside State Software and a few other shops, unnamed and unspecified.

No mediator named; edge stands, provisional.

ecma-262-third-edition-1999.name: ECMA-262 third edition
ecma-262-third-edition-1999.definition: The December 1999 ECMAScript standard, the edition RFC 4627 cites as JSON's basis.
ecma-262-third-edition-1999.bottleneck: Before ECMA-262 third edition, JavaScript's literal grammar could not be cited as the basis of another standard, because it existed only as divergent vendor behavior.
ecma-262-third-edition-1999.leap: The December 1999 edition froze the language - including the object and array literal productions - into the stable vendor-neutral text that became the decade's baseline and JSON's cited basis.
ecma-262-third-edition-1999.prior_state: Two divergent implementations (JavaScript and JScript) and a 1997 first edition already drifting from practice.

No mediator named; edge stands, provisional.

javascript-1995.name: JavaScript
javascript-1995.definition: Eich's 1995 browser language (Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript) whose literal subset JSON is.
javascript-1995.bottleneck: Before JavaScript, browsers could not execute a data notation natively, because pages were static documents with no deployed scripting language whose literals a server could reuse as data.
javascript-1995.leap: Eich's ten-day prototype (May 1995), shipped in Navigator 2.0 that September, put a C-syntax language with first-class object and array literals into every browser - the notation JSON was later discovered inside and extracted from.
javascript-1995.prior_state: Static HTML pages; interactivity via CGI round-trips, Java applets, or proprietary plug-ins.

windows-graphics-foundation-direct3d-10-.name: Windows Graphics Foundation / Direct3D 10 specification effort
windows-graphics-foundation-direct3d-10-.definition: Microsoft's next-generation graphics API effort (WGF 2.0, later Direct3D 10), designed with hardware vendors from about 2002 and circulated to IHVs in draft form well before its November 2006 release alongside Windows Vista.
windows-graphics-foundation-direct3d-10-.bottleneck: Before the Direct3D 10 specification effort, a PC GPU's feature set was a negotiation of optional capability bits, because DirectX 9 described separate vertex and pixel machines and let every vendor subset them.
windows-graphics-foundation-direct3d-10-.leap: Microsoft's WGF/Direct3D 10 effort (designed with the hardware vendors from about 2002, circulated in draft through the G80's design years) re-posed the GPU as one common shader core with a geometry stage and a guaranteed feature set - the specification the G80 was designed against and served as reference hardware for.
windows-graphics-foundation-direct3d-10-.prior_state: DirectX 9's split shader models, per-vendor capability bits, and no geometry processing stage.

lambda-calculus-1936.leap: Church's lambda calculus (mature form, 1936) made binding, substitution and function values formal objects: the specification that any language of first-class lexically-scoped functions must implement.
lambda-calculus-1936.prior_state: Informal mathematical practice with functions; combinatory logic as the only rival formalism.

(1) NOTATION-ONLY ATTACK (the strongest): McCarthy's own retrospective says he took Church's lambda notation because 'to use functions as arguments, one needs a notation for functions', adding 'I didn't understand the rest of the book, so I wasn't tempted to try to implement his more general mechanism for defining functions.' Answered: what the parent's section 2e takes from Church [3] is the function/form DISTINCTION together with the notation — the conceptual apparatus (bound and free variables, functions as values that forms apply) that constitutes the parent's function mechanism; the parent's functions ARE lambda expressions and its eval is defined over them. This is the Fisher 1918 at Fisher & Mackenzie shape: the child's central form is the ancestor's mechanism in new dress. What McCarthy did NOT take — conversion as the computation mechanism — is what the parent's eval replaces, which is the ancestor-modified relation, not independence. Attack fails; Q3 was nevertheless scored only partial at evaluation on exactly this testimony, and that scoring stands. (2) MEDIATION ATTACK via Kleene: Church and Kleene were collaborators (Kleene was Church's student; the equivalence of the calculi dates to 1936), so the Church channel might be the Kleene channel in disguise. Answered by the components split, which the parent's own text enforces: section 2e cites Church for the function form; the introduction frames the system on the partial-recursive-function scheme. Two separable components, two channels, both admitted with the split recorded; equivalence of the formalisms does not merge their channels into this parent. Attack fails. (3) SCOPING DIVERGENCE: the implemented Lisp used dynamic binding, not the lexical discipline of Church's calculus (and of this node's own stored leap text, written for the Scheme line). Recorded as part of the ancestor-modified finding: the parent deviates from Church substantially in evaluation discipline while taking the form; the edge is to the calculus as the source of the function concept and notation, which is what the parent's documents claim. actor-model-1973.name: Actor model
actor-model-1973.definition: Carl Hewitt's formalism (1973, with Bishop and Steiger): computation as actors that, on receiving a message, can send messages, create actors and designate their replacement behavior - proposed as the universal basis for modular AI systems.
actor-model-1973.bottleneck: Before the Actor model, modular AI programs had no single formalism: knowledge, control and data structures were separate ad-hoc mechanisms, and the Planner line's languages kept accumulating special control structures.
actor-model-1973.leap: Hewitt's Actor model (1973) proposed one primitive - actors that create actors, send messages and designate their next behavior - as the universal basis for modular AI systems.
actor-model-1973.prior_state: PLANNER's pattern-directed theorem proving and the proliferating special-purpose control structures of the Planner-derived languages.

algol-60-1960.name: ALGOL 60
algol-60-1960.definition: The algorithmic language of the 1960 Revised Report (Naur et al.), whose block structure made lexical scoping the discipline of an implemented language - the example from which, per the record, Sussman imported lexical scoping into Lisp.

algol-60-1960.leap: ALGOL 60 (1960) made block structure and lexical scope the discipline of a real, implemented language - the worked example of lexically-scoped programming available to be transplanted into Lisp.
algol-60-1960.prior_state: Languages with dynamic or purely stack-disciplined binding; lexical binding confined to a mathematical formalism.

conservative-policy-iteration-kakade-lan.name: Conservative policy iteration (Kakade & Langford)

policy-iteration-howard-1960.name: Policy iteration (Howard)
policy-iteration-howard-1960.definition: Ronald Howard's policy iteration (in 'Dynamic Programming and Markov Processes', 1960): alternate exact policy evaluation with greedy policy improvement; Howard proved the procedure reaches an optimal policy in finitely many iterations - the exact algorithm the parent makes approximate and certifies.
policy-iteration-howard-1960.bottleneck: Before Howard (1960), computing an optimal policy for a discounted MDP meant value iteration - an asymptotic procedure with no finite termination - or solving the optimality equations directly; there was no finite exact algorithm that improved a policy step by step.
policy-iteration-howard-1960.leap: Howard's policy iteration (1960): alternate exact evaluation of the current policy with greedy improvement against it, and the procedure reaches an optimal policy in finitely many iterations - the exact skeleton that approximate policy iteration, and this parent, are modifications of.

sparse-sampling-kearns-mansour-ng-1999.name: Sparse sampling (Kearns, Mansour & Ng)

sparse-sampling-kearns-mansour-ng-1999.bottleneck: Before Kearns, Mansour & Ng (1999), planning in an MDP was costed in the size of the state space: lookahead and value computation touched states in proportion to |S|, so large-state planning had no sample-based route with a state-space-independent guarantee.
sparse-sampling-kearns-mansour-ng-1999.leap: Sparse sampling (IJCAI 1999): given a generative model of the MDP, build a sparse sampled lookahead tree whose size depends on the horizon and the accuracy target but not on the number of states, and act near-optimally - the first planning guarantee independent of state-space size, and the paper that defined the generative-model access instrument.

complexity-of-reinforcement-learning-whi.name: Complexity of reinforcement learning (Whitehead)
complexity-of-reinforcement-learning-whi.definition: Steven Whitehead, 'Complexity and the Value of Time' (AAAI 1991) and the associated complexity analyses: reinforcement learning problems on which any learning rule can be forced to need exponentially many samples - the founding statement of RL's sample-complexity problem.

advantage-updating-baird-1993.name: Advantage updating (Baird)
advantage-updating-baird-1993.definition: Leemon Baird's 'Advantage Updating' (Wright Laboratory technical report WL-TR-93-1146, 1993): learn the advantage function A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s) instead of absolute action values, so that updates are invariant to the value offset and remain well-behaved at fine time discretizations where Q-learning degrades.
advantage-updating-baird-1993.bottleneck: Before Baird (1993), value-based learners represented absolute action values Q(s,a); as the time discretization refines, the differences between actions' Q-values shrink toward zero while their common level does not, so the learnable signal drowns in the offset - and no representation separated the two.
advantage-updating-baird-1993.leap: Baird's advantage updating (1993): learn the advantage function A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s) - how much better an action is than the policy's own average - instead of absolute values. The representation is invariant to the value offset and stays well-defined in the fine-discretization limit; the advantage becomes the object a policy improvement step is built from, which is exactly the quantity this parent's Theorem 1 bounds.
advantage-updating-baird-1993.prior_state: Absolute action-value representations (Q-learning and kin) with the offset pathology unseparated.

simula-67-1967.name: Simula 67

byte-pair-encoding-compression-algorithm.name: Byte-pair encoding compression algorithm (Gage, 1994)
byte-pair-encoding-compression-algorithm.definition: Byte-pair encoding (Philip Gage, C Users Journal, 1994): a data compression algorithm that iteratively replaces the most frequent pair of bytes in a sequence with a single unused byte, building a table of pair substitutions that shrinks the data.

byte-pair-encoding-compression-algorithm.leap: Gage's byte-pair encoding (C Users Journal, 1994): iteratively replace the most frequent adjacent byte pair in the data with a single unused byte, recording each merge - a merge table learned from the data that encodes any byte sequence over a bounded symbol set.
byte-pair-encoding-compression-algorithm.prior_state: Static-dictionary and codebook compressors (LZ-family, Huffman coding) whose tables are not learned pair-merge inventories.

serial-order-recurrent-network-jordan-19.name: Serial-order recurrent network (Jordan, 1986)
serial-order-recurrent-network-jordan-19.definition: Jordan's serial-order network (ICS Report 8604, UCSD, 1986): a recurrent network for producing sequences, in which plan units and feedback from the output layer ('state units') give the network a context for the next element - the first PDP proposal for dynamic memory through recurrence.
serial-order-recurrent-network-jordan-19.bottleneck: Before Jordan (1986), parallel distributed processing had no mechanism for serial order: feedforward networks mapped static inputs to static outputs, and Lashley's problem - how a system produces and comprehends sequences whose elements depend on unbounded context - had no connectionist answer.
serial-order-recurrent-network-jordan-19.leap: Jordan's serial-order network (ICS Report 8604, 1986): plan units plus recurrent feedback from the output layer through 'state units' give the network a dynamic memory - its own prior behavior becomes context for the next element, making sequence production a learnable network behavior.

act-1-lieberman-1981-1981.name: Act 1 (Lieberman, 1981)
act-1-lieberman-1981-1981.definition: Lieberman's Act 1 concurrent programming language (MIT AI Memo 626, May 1981; chapter in Yonezawa & Tokoro's Object-Oriented Concurrent Programming), whose objects share behavior by delegating messages to more general actors.
act-1-lieberman-1981-1981.bottleneck: Before Act 1, message-passing object systems shared behavior through classes (or not at all): there was no working language in which an individual object could concentrate generally useful behavior and let more specific objects inherit it by delegation, without a class taxonomy.
act-1-lieberman-1981-1981.leap: Act 1 (Lieberman, AI Memo 626, 1981) is a concurrent actor language whose objects use delegation: 'Act 1 uses the technique of delegating messages, which allows concentrating shared knowledge in actors with very general behavior, and creating extensions of these actors with idiosyncratic behavior' - the practice Lieberman's 1986 paper abstracts into the general mechanism.
act-1-lieberman-1981-1981.prior_state: The actor model without a sharing mechanism (actors as isolated message processors); class-based sharing in Simula/Smalltalk as the only worked-out alternative.

applied-optimal-control-bryson-ho-1969-1.name: Applied Optimal Control (Bryson & Ho, 1969)
applied-optimal-control-bryson-ho-1969-1.definition: Bryson and Ho's 1969 textbook codifying the Kelley-Bryson multistage gradient procedure - adjoint equations and Lagrange-multiplier recursions for gradients through dynamical systems - the standard form of first-generation backwards differentiation in optimal control.
applied-optimal-control-bryson-ho-1969-1.bottleneck: Computing the gradient of a trajectory objective with respect to controls or parameters required re-deriving sensitivity equations problem by problem; no standard codified procedure existed for multistage systems.
applied-optimal-control-bryson-ho-1969-1.leap: Bryson & Ho (1969) codify the Kelley-Bryson gradient procedure - adjoint equations and Lagrange-multiplier recursions giving gradients through arbitrary multistage dynamical systems - as the standard textbook method of first-generation backwards differentiation.
applied-optimal-control-bryson-ho-1969-1.prior_state: Variational calculus and Pontryagin-style necessary conditions stated problem by problem; Kelley's 1960 adjoint derivation known mainly inside the flight-mechanics community.

statistical-decision-functions-wald-1950.name: Statistical Decision Functions (Wald, 1950)
statistical-decision-functions-wald-1950.definition: Abraham Wald's 1950 monograph founding statistical decision theory: decisions under uncertainty as optimization over decision functions, including the sequential (multi-stage) case - the framework Bellman's 1952 founding note names as dynamic programming's intimate relative.
statistical-decision-functions-wald-1950.bottleneck: Decisions under uncertainty had no general theory: statistical inference, sequential experimentation, and choice under risk were separate crafts with no common optimization frame.
statistical-decision-functions-wald-1950.leap: Wald (1950) founds statistical decision theory: a decision problem is an optimization over decision functions against a loss, with sequential problems as staged decisions - the frame Bellman's programme generalizes from inference to control.
statistical-decision-functions-wald-1950.prior_state: Classical estimation and testing theory (Neyman-Pearson) without a decision-theoretic optimization frame.

bayes-and-minimax-solutions-of-sequentia.name: Bayes and Minimax Solutions of Sequential Decision Problems (Arrow, Blackwell & Girshick, 1949)
bayes-and-minimax-solutions-of-sequentia.definition: Arrow, Blackwell and Girshick's 1949 Econometrica paper solving sequential decision problems (Bayes and minimax) by a recursive stage-by-stage construction - the earliest backward-induction solution of a multistage decision problem in the literature Bellman cites.
bayes-and-minimax-solutions-of-sequentia.bottleneck: Sequential statistical decisions had no solution method: how to choose at each stage, knowing later stages remain, was unformalized.
bayes-and-minimax-solutions-of-sequentia.leap: Arrow, Blackwell & Girshick (1949) solve sequential decision problems by backward recursion over decision regions - the DP recursion operating in the statistical setting, eight years before the monograph.
bayes-and-minimax-solutions-of-sequentia.prior_state: Wald's sequential analysis for the special case of tests and stopping; no general recursive solution for sequential decisions.

rand-corporation-1948-1948.name: RAND Corporation (1948)
rand-corporation-1948-1948.definition: The RAND Corporation (founded 1948), where Bellman developed dynamic programming: the monograph is a RAND research study, and the DP report programme (R-245, R-271, and the journal papers) is the institutional output the book collects.

simula-i-1965.name: Simula I
simula-i-1965.definition: Dahl & Nygaard's discrete-event simulation language (designed 1962-64, operational on the UNIVAC 1107 by January 1965, CACM 1966): ALGOL 60 plus activity/process declarations whose block instances escaped the stack discipline - the direct precursor Simula 67 generalized.
simula-i-1965.bottleneck: Before Simula I, describing a discrete-event system meant hand-coding its processes and event scheduling in a general-purpose language: there was no language whose components were the system's own processes, carrying data and actions over simulated time.
simula-i-1965.leap: Simula I (operational 1965; CACM 1966) makes the system's processes the program's components: activity declarations give block instances an independent existence off the stack, referenced explicitly, inspectable from outside, and sequenced quasi-parallel over simulated time.
simula-i-1965.prior_state: Hand-built simulation code in FORTRAN or ALGOL; special-purpose simulation packages without process structure.
