lashley-the-problem-of-serial-order-in-b.name: Lashley, The problem of serial order in behavior (1951)
lashley-the-problem-of-serial-order-in-b.definition: Karl Lashley's 1951 Hixon Symposium chapter: the founding formulation of the serial-order problem — associative chaining cannot explain ordered behavior (no mechanism chooses among an element's outgoing links; anticipatory/context effects are unaccounted), so sequences must be organized by central, parallel schemata.
lashley-the-problem-of-serial-order-in-b.bottleneck: Before Lashley (1951), serially ordered behavior had no posed problem, because chaining was assumed sufficient and the branching ambiguity of chained elements and the anticipatory overlap of real sequences were invisible as design constraints.
lashley-the-problem-of-serial-order-in-b.leap: Lashley (1951) formulated the serial-order problem: he refuted associative chaining — an element with several possible successors cannot choose among them, and future actions demonstrably influence present ones — and required central, parallel organization instead, the formulation every later serial-order theory works inside.
lashley-the-problem-of-serial-order-in-b.prior_state: Associative chaining as the unexamined default: each action triggered by its predecessor, order stored in the links themselves.

sources.title: Jordan, Serial Order: A Parallel Distributed Processing Approach (ICS Report 8604, UCSD, May 1986) — the parent report's own text

verification.notes: Three attacks run. (1) Mediation attack — the strongest: does Lashley reach the parent through Wickelgren (1969) or through Rumelhart & Norman (1982), the frame's attempted solutions? Refused on the parent's documents: the report's Serial Order section engages Lashley's two refutations directly and separately ('Many of the problems... were anticipated by Lashley (1951)'), then treats Wickelgren as the solution that 'solves the problems posed by Lashley' and fails on further grounds — the constraints and the attempted solutions are distinct channels in the text itself, and Wickelgren was evaluated and rejected at this same parent on the mechanism-retention discrimination. (2) Q-gate attack: Lashley solved nothing — Q1 is partial and the admission rests on Q2 (generativity of the formulation) plus documentary necessity. This is the problem-side shape of the Bateson-1909-at-Fisher-1918 admission (the carrier of the problem formulation the paper supposes), and of the Charter-at-GPT-2 rule that a specific document can carry an era condition: here the document carries the problem itself, and the parent's text instantiates its two constraints as design requirements (state vector for branching; output generalization for anticipation). It is flagged as this expansion's most contestable call: a reader who requires problem-formulations to clear Q1 rather than Q2 would kill this edge. (3) Multiples test: no rival formulation of the serial-order problem from the era is on record; the Hixon symposium context makes Lashley's the canonical statement, and the field's survey literature (Houghton & Hartley, 'Lashley Revisited', 1995) organizes the lineage as returns to it. Necessity is therefore documentary-historical, scored Q3 partial, not logical. Outcome provisional.

rumelhart-norman-simulating-a-skilled-ty.name: Rumelhart & Norman, Simulating a skilled typist: A study of skilled cognitive-motor performance (1982)
rumelhart-norman-simulating-a-skilled-ty.definition: Rumelhart & Norman's 1982 typing model (Cognitive Science 6): words as schemata whose letter control elements are activated in parallel, with temporal order imposed by lateral inhibitory connections among elements that precede one another — the PDP programme's first parallel model of serial behavior.
rumelhart-norman-simulating-a-skilled-ty.bottleneck: Before Rumelhart & Norman (1982), parallel distributed processing had no model of serial behavior at all, because its networks mapped static patterns to static patterns and skilled sequential performance lay outside the programme.
rumelhart-norman-simulating-a-skilled-ty.leap: The typing model (1982) made serial behavior PDP-modelable: word schemata activate letter elements in parallel and lateral inhibition orders them, reproducing the overlapping keystrokes of transcription typing — the first parallel model of a skilled sequence, and the platform the parent's state/output theory modifies.
rumelhart-norman-simulating-a-skilled-ty.prior_state: Serial order handled by symbolic buffers and program counters, or by chaining; PDP models were static pattern associators.

sources.title: Jordan, Serial Order: A Parallel Distributed Processing Approach (ICS Report 8604, UCSD, May 1986) — the parent report's own text

verification.notes: Three attacks run. (1) Mediation attack: does the typing model reach the parent through the PDP volumes (1986), which discuss it? Refused on chronology and artifact identity: the candidate is the 1982 Cognitive Science journal article, a separable artifact the parent cites directly and argues with section by section; the volumes are a later codification, dated to the parent's own year and date-dropped at this resolve in any case — the channel runs article to parent, not volume to parent. (2) Multiples / necessity attack: Grossberg's graded-activation schemes (1978) were a live alternative ancestor, so necessity is ripe and Q3 is scored partial as recorded; the discrimination between the two is mechanism retention — the parent keeps Rumelhart & Norman's parallel activation with generalization and replaces only the ordering device, whereas Grossberg's graded-activation principle is itself superseded by the state/output split and grouped by the parent with the schemes its repeated-element objection covers. (3) Q1 attack: the model solved typing, not serial order — recorded as Q1 partial; the edge rests on Q2 (it made serial behavior PDP-modelable, the space the parent enters) plus the ancestor-modified relation documented in the parent's own argument (adoption of parallel activation; the three failures — repeated elements, doubling, parser breaks in ABCA — that the state vector repairs). No stronger attack found. Outcome provisional.

renderman-shading-language-hanrahan-laws.name: RenderMan Shading Language (Hanrahan & Lawson, 1990)
renderman-shading-language-hanrahan-laws.definition: The shading language of Pixar's RenderMan, published as Hanrahan & Lawson, 'A Language for Shading and Lighting Calculations' (SIGGRAPH 1990): a C-like procedural language in which surface, light, displacement and volume shaders are written once and executed by the renderer, with a standard library of graphics primitives.
renderman-shading-language-hanrahan-laws.bottleneck: Before RenderMan SL, a renderer's shading was fixed by its implementers, because no user-writable language existed in which appearance could be programmed per production.
renderman-shading-language-hanrahan-laws.leap: Hanrahan & Lawson (1990) made shading a language: appearance became portable, user-authored procedural code - surface and light shaders - instead of renderer internals.
renderman-shading-language-hanrahan-laws.prior_state: Hard-coded shading models inside renderers; Cook's shade trees as a research formulation without a production language.

sources.title: Hanrahan & Lawson, SIGGRAPH 1990; Proudfoot, Mark, Tzvetkov & Hanrahan, A Real-Time Procedural Shading System for Programmable Graphics Hardware, Proc. SIGGRAPH 2001 (introduction and related work); Mark, Stanford RTSL SIGGRAPH 2001 course notes (April 18, 2001), graphics.stanford.edu/courses and the RTSL project page (graphics.stanford.edu/papers/rtsl/)

verification.notes: Four attacks run on the RenderMan SL -> RTSL edge (7.5), the deferred hearing discharged this session. (1) Q1 attack partially lands on the node's broad form: Cook's shade trees (1984) had already formulated shading as composable procedure, so 'shading becomes programmable' is not SL's flip alone. It fails on the edge-scoped form: what the parent presupposes and consumes is not the formulation but the reigning LANGUAGE - shader kinds as a textual language with a standard library, in production use for a decade ('the most common shading language in use today', in the parent's own words). The edge stands on that form. (2) Multiples test on Q3: PixelFlow/pfman (1998) and ISL (2000) independently carried shading languages toward hardware in the parent's era, so the necessity of the parent's TRANSFER is ripe - already scored Q3 partial, and the cap stands. But as an attack on THIS edge it misfires: both multiples themselves take SL as their language model (pfman is 'a RenderMan-like language'; ISL compiles the RenderMan language), so the parallels reinforce the SL channel rather than rival it. (3) Date and direction check out: Hanrahan & Lawson, SIGGRAPH 1990, a decade before the parent; direction documented by the parent's text and by Hanrahan's authorship on both papers. (4) Mediation attack, three mediators tried. Via the RenderMan Interface Specification: refused - the parent implements no RenderMan interface and compiles to GPU back ends, not RIB; the specification contains a language definition, and containment is not a channel (the RISpec rejection records this). Via Cook's shade trees: refused as complete mediation - SL is not a transparent conduit for the 1984 formulation; what the parent consumes (shader kinds as a textual language, the library design, the production practice) is SL's own contribution, and the senior author's personal channel bypasses 1984 entirely; Cook is recorded as mediated via SL, the chain carried by its cited final link. Via Advanced RenderMan (1999): refused - documentation of the mediator, and the channel here is the designer himself. Strongest standing caveat: the Q3 partial (the transfer was ripe; the edge rests on the specificity of the design consumed and the documented channel, not on necessity). Outcome provisional, per the run's standing (no node is verified); no mediation object - no attack killed or downgraded the edge.

perlin-an-image-synthesizer-1985-1985.name: Perlin, An Image Synthesizer (1985)
perlin-an-image-synthesizer-1985-1985.definition: Ken Perlin's 'An Image Synthesizer' (SIGGRAPH 1985): a pixel-stream shading language with conditional and looping constructs, function and procedure definitions, and the procedural noise and turbulence functions that became the standard vocabulary of procedural shading.
perlin-an-image-synthesizer-1985-1985.bottleneck: Before Perlin's synthesizer, procedural shading had no full language and no compact computable primitive for natural irregularity, because shade formulations lacked control flow, functions and a noise primitive.
perlin-an-image-synthesizer-1985-1985.leap: Perlin (1985) carried procedural shading into a full language - conditionals, loops, functions - and gave it the noise primitive every later shading library inherited.
perlin-an-image-synthesizer-1985-1985.prior_state: Cook's shade trees as an expression formulation without control flow or function definitions.

sources.title: Hanrahan & Lawson, 'A Language for Shading and Lighting Calculations', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1990 (abstract and introduction); Olano (2014): 'In 1985, Ken Perlin's Image Synthesizer expanded this into a full language, with functions, loops and branching'

verification.notes: Four attacks run on the Perlin (1985) -> RenderMan SL edge (6.0). (1) Q1 attack: partially lands on the broad claim - Cook had posed procedural shading a year earlier, so Perlin did not flip shading from impossible to posable. It fails on the edge-scoped form: the flip THIS edge carries is from formulation to full language (conditionals, loops, function definitions, the noise primitive), and the parent paper's introduction enumerates exactly those constructs as Perlin's contribution. (2) Multiples test on Q3: Peachey's solid texturing (same year, 1985) is the parallel technique-side statement of the same stratum - recorded at this expansion as mediated via this candidate (the stratum's language-side carrier), and Q3 was already scored partial. No further downgrade. (3) Date and direction check out: SIGGRAPH 1985; the parent paper states it 'incorporates features of both Cook's and Perlin's systems'. (4) Mediation attack: via Cook refused (distinct components - the synthesizer's constructs are not Cook's content carried forward; Perlin's paper is an independent construction); via Peachey refused on direction (a parallel, not an intermediary). No mediation object. Strongest standing caveat: the Q3 partial - the parent merges two ancestors, and this edge rests on the specificity of the constructs consumed, not on sole necessity. Outcome provisional.

reyes-rendering-architecture-cook-carpen.name: REYES rendering architecture (Cook, Carpenter & Catmull, 1987)
reyes-rendering-architecture-cook-carpen.definition: The REYES architecture ('Renders Everything You Ever Saw', Cook, Carpenter & Catmull, SIGGRAPH 1987): primitives are diced into micropolygon grids, shaded as whole grids, then sampled - the architecture Pixar's renderer implemented and the one the RenderMan Interface was designed around.
reyes-rendering-architecture-cook-carpen.bottleneck: Before REYES, film-quality rendering had no unified architecture, because geometry, shading and sampling were handled by incompatible special-purpose code.
reyes-rendering-architecture-cook-carpen.leap: Cook, Carpenter & Catmull (1987) unified film rendering in one micropolygon architecture whose shading stage is executed per grid - the execution world the RenderMan Shading Language was designed for.
reyes-rendering-architecture-cook-carpen.prior_state: Ad hoc production renderers with hard-coded shading; ray tracers too slow for feature-film complexity.

sources.title: ACM Turing Award profile of Pat Hanrahan: 'Hanrahan's team built RenderMan on top of a system previously developed by Catmull along with Loren Carpenter and Rob Cook called REYES'; RenderMan Interface Specification schematic: 'REYES is where RenderMan started... the architecture the RenderMan Interface Specification was designed around... it shaped the spec's semantics, including ShadingRate, the shading-before-visibility order'

verification.notes: Four attacks run on the REYES (1987) -> RenderMan SL edge (6.0). (1) Q1 attack: lands on the broad form, as scored - REYES did not make shading programmable (Q1 was scored partial for exactly this); the edge-scoped claim is narrower and stands: the parent language's execution semantics (whole micropolygon grids shaded at once, derivatives across grid neighbours, shading before visibility) are the architecture's semantics, and a production language of this form has no referent without them. (2) Multiples test on Q3: renderer architectures were multiple in the era (production ray tracers, ad hoc film renderers) - the REYES bet was one of several, and Q3 was scored partial; the edge rests on this language's documented design target, not on the architecture's uniqueness. (3) Date and direction check out: SIGGRAPH 1987; the language was built at Pixar by the RISpec's architect as the shading component of the REYES renderer (ACM record: Hanrahan's team 'built RenderMan on top of' REYES). (4) Mediation attack - the strongest available: via the RenderMan Interface Specification, on the ground that the language's renderer interface is specified IN the spec, so the architecture might reach the language only through the document. Refused: the dependency runs the other way - the spec 'was designed around' REYES and codified the architecture's pre-existing semantics (ShadingRate, shading-before-visibility); Hanrahan implemented the language in the REYES renderer itself (PRMan), not in the document; and a container of the child, refused at this same parent on containment, cannot simultaneously be the carrier of the child's edge from its design target. No mediation object. Outcome provisional; the Q3 partial is the standing caveat.

cook-shade-trees-1984-1984.name: Cook, Shade Trees (1984)
cook-shade-trees-1984-1984.definition: Robert L. Cook's 'Shade Trees' (SIGGRAPH 1984): shading described as a tree of procedural nodes evaluated per visible point, with light source specification, surface reflectance and atmospheric effects separated as conceptually independent tasks - the founding formulation of programmable procedural shading.
cook-shade-trees-1984-1984.bottleneck: Before shade trees, shading was a fixed computation inside each renderer, because no formulation separated the shading computation into composable procedural parts.
cook-shade-trees-1984-1984.leap: Cook (1984) formulated shading as an evaluable tree of procedures with separated shader kinds - the model from which shading languages developed.
cook-shade-trees-1984-1984.prior_state: Fixed illumination models (Phong and kin) implemented as renderer code.

sources.title: Hanrahan & Lawson, 'A Language for Shading and Lighting Calculations', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1990 (abstract and introduction); Olano, 'Early stories of shading on graphics hardware' (2014): 'It also introduced the shader types of surface, light, atmosphere, etc. still present in RenderMan today'
Perlin, 'An Image Synthesizer', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1985 (introduction, ref [1]); Heckbert, 'Survey of Texture Mapping', IEEE CG&A Nov 1986
Cook, Carpenter & Catmull, 'The Reyes Image Rendering Architecture', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1987 (introduction; design assumptions; ref [11])

verification.notes: THIS EXPANSION'S MOST CONTESTABLE CALL - flagged for the record. The admission rests on a discrimination: the shader model is not a component technique consumed by the architecture (the Blinn-1978-at-Perlin shape) but the presupposition of its central design decision (grids shaded together before visibility), supported by the paper's own necessity language ('we consider a programmable shader a necessity') and its constituent list ('algorithms that were developed for the Reyes architecture... shade trees [11]'). Attack: a fixed-shader micropolygon renderer is demonstrably conceivable - the predecessor production renderers were exactly that - and the evaluation already capped Q3 at partial on this ground; the attack does not reach the directness record, which is a different-form counterfactual, not an impossibility claim. Mediation attack: via Perlin 1985 (the other shading-language formulation) - refused; Cook first-authors the parent, the paper cites shade trees directly, and the Reyes shading stage descends from Cook's own formulation, not through Perlin's pixel-stream variant (the two are separate children of Cook in this graph). RE-HEARING CONDITION: a document showing the 1987 architecture's shading stage was designed independently of the shade-tree model (e.g. an early Reyes design with fixed shaders only, the model added later) would downgrade this edge to a consumed-component record.

ferraro-functional-composition-for-textu.name: Ferraro, functional composition for texture (personal communication, c. 1984)
ferraro-functional-composition-for-textu.definition: Mike Ferraro's suggestion (personal communication, before 1985) that texture be created by functional composition - the concept the parent paper's acknowledgements credit as the work's root: 'Mike Ferraro originated the crucial concept of using functional composition to create texture. Much of this paper has its roots in his powerful idea.'
ferraro-functional-composition-for-textu.bottleneck: Before Ferraro's suggestion, procedural texture had no founding design principle, because textures were made by mapping stored images or by growing models rather than by composing functions.
ferraro-functional-composition-for-textu.leap: Ferraro (personal communication, before 1985) proposed that texture be created by functional composition - the concept Perlin's synthesizer paper credits as its root: 'Much of this paper has its roots in his powerful idea.'
ferraro-functional-composition-for-textu.prior_state: Texture made by conventional texture mapping or growth-model algorithms (the parent abstract's own contrast).

sources.title: Perlin, 'An Image Synthesizer', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1985 (abstract; Acknowledgements; ref [13])

verification.notes: THIS EXPANSION'S MOST CONTESTABLE CALL - flagged for the record. Q2 attack: partially lands - the abstract names two ingredients (composition of nonlinear functions AND 'powerful primitives for creating controlled stochastic effects'); the composition principle alone, without the author's noise primitive, would not have produced the parent. The edge survives the attack because the evaluation's claim is scoped to the concept channel, and the paper's acknowledgement is unusually specific testimony ('originated the crucial concept', 'Much of this paper has its roots in his powerful idea'), not a courtesy credit. Multiples test on Q3: Cook's published shade trees (1984) already compose procedures, and Williams pursued a parallel line - necessity was capped at partial in the evaluation on this ground. Date/direction attack: the communication is undated (filed c. 1984 from ref [13]); the direction is attested by the child itself, which is the strongest available evidence and the reason the edge exists at all. Mediation attack: via Cook's paper - refused; no evidence the concept reached Perlin through the published trees, and the paper cites Cook for a different component (the expression-parser formulation). RE-HEARING CONDITION: any dated document showing Perlin composing functions for texture before contact with Ferraro, or showing the concept arriving via Cook 1984, kills this edge and re-files Ferraro as a multiple.

catmull-a-subdivision-algorithm-for-comp.name: Catmull, A Subdivision Algorithm for Computer Display of Curved Surfaces (1974)
catmull-a-subdivision-algorithm-for-comp.definition: Edwin Catmull's University of Utah PhD dissertation (Dec 1974): subdivision display of curved surfaces, and the dissertation that also introduced the z-buffer and texture mapping for curved surfaces.
catmull-a-subdivision-algorithm-for-comp.bottleneck: Before Catmull's dissertation, curved surfaces could not be displayed directly, because rendering worked on polygons and visibility had no per-pixel depth method.
catmull-a-subdivision-algorithm-for-comp.leap: Catmull (1974) founded patch-based rendering: subdivision display of curved surfaces, the z-buffer, and texture mapping - the three inventions the Reyes architecture's stages run on.
catmull-a-subdivision-algorithm-for-comp.prior_state: Polygonal approximation modelled by hand; painter's and scanline visibility methods.

sources.title: Cook, Carpenter & Catmull, 'The Reyes Image Rendering Architecture', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1987 (ref [8]); Catmull dissertation record

verification.notes: Q1 attack: lands only as already recorded - the evaluation scoped the flip as inherited (partial), since the architecture presupposes patch rendering rather than flipping it. Multiples test on Q3: Strasser's independent z-buffer (1974) is the standing multiple and was the stated reason Q3 is partial; no further downgrade - the paper cites THIS dissertation [8] and its author co-authors the parent. Date/direction: 1974 -> 1987, direction documented by direct citation. Mediation attack: via Lane et al. (1980) for the subdivision strand - refused; the paper names Lane-Carpenter as an ANALOGY for dicing ('similar to'), while the dissertation is the cited source for the trio (subdivision, z-buffer, texture mapping) and the z-buffer/texture strands have no Lane-Carpenter path at all. Outcome provisional per run convention.

cook-stochastic-sampling-in-computer-gra.name: Cook, Stochastic Sampling in Computer Graphics (1986)
cook-stochastic-sampling-in-computer-gra.definition: Robert L. Cook's 'Stochastic Sampling in Computer Graphics' (ACM TOG 1986): Monte Carlo (jittered) point sampling for antialiasing and the integration of motion blur and depth of field.
cook-stochastic-sampling-in-computer-gra.bottleneck: Before stochastic sampling, antialiasing and blur in renderers required supersampling or separate passes, because sample placement was regular and effects were not integrated in the sampling step.
cook-stochastic-sampling-in-computer-gra.leap: Cook (1986) made visibility and image integration a Monte Carlo sampling problem: jittered point samples integrate antialiasing, motion blur and depth of field in one pass.
cook-stochastic-sampling-in-computer-gra.prior_state: Regular sampling; ray tracers integrating blur at prohibitive cost; scanline renderers without blur.

sources.title: Cook, Carpenter & Catmull, 'The Reyes Image Rendering Architecture', Proc. SIGGRAPH 1987 (abstract; hider section; ref [12])

verification.notes: Q1 attack: the scoped flip (blur integrated in a scanline hider's sampling step) survives - no pre-1986 micropolygon/scanline renderer integrating motion blur and depth of field in its visibility sampling was found; the paper's mechanism (micropolygons moved to jittered times/lens positions per sample) is this candidate's method. Multiples test on Q3: jittered sampling was a named technique in the air ('a type of stochastic sampling called jittering'), and Q3 was capped partial accordingly. Mediation attack: via distributed ray tracing (1984) - refused; DRT distributes RAYS for shading effects, while the hider's jittered POINT sampling of micropolygons is the 1986 paper's subject, and the parent cites [12] as the sampling method's source ('described in detail elsewhere'). Date/direction: TOG Jan 1986 -> SIGGRAPH 1987, direction by incorporation-by-reference. The ISL discrimination (whole stage's defining method vs a fallback-path technique) is recorded in the evaluation. Outcome provisional per run convention.

t5-text-to-text-transfer-transformer-201.name: T5 (text-to-text transfer transformer)
t5-text-to-text-transfer-transformer-201.definition: Raffel et al. (2019): a single encoder-decoder transformer trained with a unified text-to-text format on C4 plus a supervised multi-task mixture, every task rendered as text in and text out.
t5-text-to-text-transfer-transformer-201.bottleneck: Before T5, multi-task NLP training was impractical as a single-model discipline because every task demanded its own architecture, output head and training regime, so transfer results could not be compared or composed.
t5-text-to-text-transfer-transformer-201.leap: T5 (2019) showed a single text-to-text transformer trained on a unified mixture (C4 pretraining plus a supervised multi-task mixture) matches or beats task-specific architectures across the benchmark suite, making format unification and mixture training a reusable, documented recipe.
t5-text-to-text-transfer-transformer-201.prior_state: Task-specific architectures and per-task fine-tuning of pretrained encoders (BERT-style); multi-task learning confined to shared-encoder models with task-specific heads (MT-DNN).

sources.title: Raffel et al., 'Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer', arXiv:1910.10683 (2019); Wei et al., 'Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners', arXiv:2109.01652 (Sep 2021)

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: T5's Q1 was scored partial at evaluation (it flipped no impossibility itself; it made the single-model multi-task training object exist) - the admission rests on Q2 (generativity of the unified format), which survives attack: every subsequent multitask/instruction system (T0, the parent) works in the text-to-text frame. (2) Multiples test on Q3: the same modification was performed independently on T5 itself by T0 (Oct 2021, AFTER the parent - a multiple in the same season, capping necessity at 'ripe', already reflected in Q3 partial); decaNLP (2018) and UnifiedQA (2020) are relatives, not multiples of the recipe. Necessity stays partial; the node does not stand on necessity grounds. (3) Date/direction: T5 is dated by its carrying publication (arXiv:1910.10683, Oct 2019); the direction T5 -> FLAN is documented in the parent paper's own mixture construction (examples-proportional mixing with a mixing-rate maximum, adopted from Raffel et al.) and its format design. (4) Mediation attack: three candidate mediators tried and refused - LaMDA-PT carries the parent's weights and architecture but not its mixture recipe or task format (the recipe channel runs paper-to-paper); T0 postdates the parent (Oct vs Sep 2021) and cannot mediate; Natural Instructions is a parallel same-year formulation whose crowdsourced instructions are not the parent's channel (the parent's templates are author-written). STRONGEST ATTACK (recorded, answered, caps at provisional): the components attack - that the text-to-text format and mixing recipe are components inside the parent's training run rather than its presupposition. Answered by the Cook-at-REYES discrimination: a component is consumed inside the leap's mechanism (a technique the run uses), while the format-plus-recipe defines what the parent's training object IS - remove it and there is no mixture to instruction-tune on, only a base model and 62 unrelated datasets. The edge stands as the parent's recipe-and-format ancestry; the attack is recorded here so a future design review can re-hear it.

orqa-latent-retrieval-for-weakly-supervi.name: ORQA: Latent Retrieval for Weakly Supervised Open Domain Question Answering
orqa-latent-retrieval-for-weakly-supervi.bottleneck: Before ORQA, open-domain QA systems could not learn retrieval from question-answer pairs alone because the evidence passage is never labelled, so retrievers were trained on heuristics or distant supervision and readers were extractive span predictors bolted onto them.
orqa-latent-retrieval-for-weakly-supervi.leap: ORQA (Lee, Chang & Toutanova, ACL 2019) made retrieval itself a latent variable trained end-to-end for open-domain QA: an Inverse Cloze Task pretrained dual-encoder retriever over Wikipedia passages, jointly fine-tuned with a BERT reader by marginalizing over retrieved evidence - and fixed the field's corpus convention (the December 2018 Wikipedia dump in passage form).
orqa-latent-retrieval-for-weakly-supervi.prior_state: Pipeline retrieve-and-extract systems (DrQA) with TF-IDF retrieval trained independently of the reader; no end-to-end latent retrieval.

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: Q1 was scored partial at evaluation (ORQA's flip is the latent-retrieval formulation, not the generative capability, which is the parent's own) - the admission rests on Q2 generativity, which survives: REALM and the parent were built in ORQA's space within a year. (2) Multiples test on Q3: REALM (Feb 2020, date-dropped here) performed the same formulation modification in parallel - a genuine multiple, already reflected in Q3 partial; the edge does not stand on necessity. (3) Date/direction: ORQA is dated by its carrying publications (arXiv:1906.00300, Jun 2019; ACL 2019); the direction ORQA -> RAG is documented in the parent's methods text ('Following Lee et al. ... we use the December 2018 dump') and introduction. (4) Mediation attack via DPR: DPR carries the parent's retriever weights and its index, but the two channels claimed for ORQA - the corpus convention and the latent-retrieval formulation - both exist inside ORQA before DPR (ORQA's retriever is ICT-pretrained, its corpus is the same dump in the same passage form), and the parent's citation for the corpus runs to Lee et al., not to Karpukhin et al. Attack fails. Strongest residual attack (recorded): that ORQA contributes 'only' the formulation while every working part of the parent comes from elsewhere (DPR's retriever, BART, the corpus artifact) - answered by the design/component distinction: a formulation is not a component inside the runs, it is what the runs instantiate; the same attack would dissolve the Cook-at-REYES presupposition edge. Outcome provisional, as for all nodes in this run.

language-models-as-knowledge-bases-lama-.name: Language Models as Knowledge Bases? (LAMA probe)
language-models-as-knowledge-bases-lama-.bottleneck: Before the LAMA probe, whether a pretrained language model's parameters function as a knowledge base was impractical to state, let alone measure, because no controlled probe separated stored relational knowledge from surface cues.
language-models-as-knowledge-bases-lama-.leap: Petroni et al. (EMNLP 2019) showed pretrained LMs do store relational knowledge retrievable by cloze queries - and, in the same programme, mapped the limits of parametric storage (no provenance, no updatability), posing the problem the parent's design answers.
language-models-as-knowledge-bases-lama-.prior_state: Language models treated as text models; their knowledge content unexamined as an object of study.

verification.notes: Four attacks run; this is the expansion's MOST CONTESTABLE admission and is flagged as such. (1) Q1 attack: partial at evaluation; the admission rests on Q2 (programme generativity: probing, KILT, knowledge editing, and the retrieval response inside the same laboratory). The Q2 attack - that the retrieval response would have happened without LAMA - cannot be fully closed; it is answered only by the documentary chain (same lab, Petroni on both papers, the parent's introduction adopting the parametric/non-parametric framing and its three failure modes as design requirements). (2) Multiples on Q3: the closed-book QA programme (Roberts et al., Feb 2020, date-dropped here) posed the same underlying question with the opposite answer - a rival, not a multiple; it strengthens that the problem was posed, not who posed it. Q3 stays partial. (3) Date/direction: EMNLP 2019 (arXiv Sep 2019), clean; direction is programme-internal and documented by authorship and framing adoption. (4) Mediation attack via ORQA/REALM: both are method papers of 2019/2020 that presuppose the problem rather than pose it; neither carries the problem document's framing into the parent - the carrier is the laboratory's own programme, whose dated document is LAMA itself. Attack fails. The Hochreiter-condition attack (diagnosis answered is not derivation) was the strongest: it is answered in the verdict by the adoption of LAMA's terms as the parent architecture's organizing distinction, but a future design review could reasonably re-hear this edge as fail-closed partial; the re-hearing condition is a showing that the parent's framing language circulated independently of the LAMA programme before Sep 2019. Outcome provisional.

asdiv-miao-et-al-2020-2020.name: ASDiv (Miao et al., 2020)
asdiv-miao-et-al-2020-2020.definition: ASDiv (Miao, Liang & Su, ACL 2020): a 2,305-problem English math word problem corpus built for diversity - problems collected from 28 websites and pruned so the corpus spans wide lexicon usage and problem types, annotated with problem type and grade level, and shipped with a lexicon-usage-diversity metric for judging corpora.
asdiv-miao-et-al-2020-2020.bottleneck: Before ASDiv, math word problem corpora were assembled by scraping or aggregation and judged by size alone, because no corpus treated diversity and quality as measurable design criteria.
asdiv-miao-et-al-2020-2020.leap: Miao, Liang & Su (2020) made corpus diversity a measurable design criterion - lexicon diversity, problem-type coverage and grade annotation - the standard GSM8K's design principles explicitly share and extend.
asdiv-miao-et-al-2020-2020.prior_state: Scraped and aggregated corpora (Dolphin18K; the MAWPS pool) judged by problem count.

sources.title: Miao, Liang & Su, 'A Diverse Corpus for Evaluating and Developing English Math Word Problem Solvers', ACL 2020; Cobbe et al., 'Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems', arXiv:2110.14168 (Oct 2021)

verification.notes: Adversarial verification, ASDiv -> GSM8K edge. (1) Q1 attack: searched for a pre-2020 carrier of corpus-diversity-as-design-criterion in the word-problem lineage - the pre-2020 corpora (MAWPS pool, Dolphin18K) were assembled by aggregation/scraping and compared by count; diversity metrics existed in other fields but no MWP corpus was built to satisfy stated diversity/quality criteria before ASDiv. Attack fails; Q1 pass stands. (2) Multiples test on Q3: Ape210K (2020) is a scale multiple, not a criteria multiple; SVAMP (2021) is built ON ASDiv-A (downstream, not independent). No second independent carrier of the criteria in the decade; Q3 stays at the partial already scored - necessity was never claimed stronger. (3) Date/direction: ACL 2020 precedes the parent's Oct 2021; direction is confirmed by the child's own text ('We share those design principles in the creation of GSM8K'), influence running from the candidate's criteria into the parent's design. (4) Mediation attack: three candidate mediators tried - MAWPS (aggregated the lineage but contributed no diversity criterion; the criteria are ASDiv's addition), Miao et al. 2021 MathQA analysis (different document, the parent's own year, about a different corpus's flaws), SVAMP/ASDiv-A (postdates the candidate, the parent's own year, never cited by the parent). None carries the criteria channel; the attack does not land. Outcome provisional per standing practice.

nvlink-interconnect-2014.name: NVLink interconnect
nvlink-interconnect-2014.definition: NVLink (announced GTC 25 Mar 2014, NVIDIA with IBM): a point-to-point GPU interconnect protocol and link, designed for 5-12x PCIe bandwidth, cache-coherent connection to IBM POWER CPUs, first integrated into Pascal-generation GPUs. The parent implements it at 160 GB/s bidirectional per GPU.
nvlink-interconnect-2014.bottleneck: Before NVLink, GPUs in a node could talk to each other only through PCIe at ~16 GB/s per direction, because no dedicated high-bandwidth GPU interconnect existed.
nvlink-interconnect-2014.leap: NVLink (announced 2014, first shipped in Pascal in 2016) gave GPUs a dedicated point-to-point interconnect at 160 GB/s bidirectional with a cache-coherent CPU endpoint - 5-12x PCIe - making the tightly coupled multi-GPU node a designable system.
nvlink-interconnect-2014.prior_state: Multi-GPU systems communicated over PCIe (x16, ~16 GB/s per direction), often through switch chips that multiplied GPU count without multiplying bandwidth.

sources.title: NVIDIA, 'NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU Architecture' whitepaper WP-08608-001_v1.1 (Aug 2017)

verification.notes: Verification of the NEW EDGE V100 -> NVLink (the node was verified at its P100 admission and expanded in this session). Four attacks. (1) Q1 attack: generation 2 extends the artifact's own 2014-16 flip rather than flipping anew - already scored partial. (2) Multiples test on Q3: AMD's Infinity Fabric (2017) is a near-simultaneous rival coherent fabric in the same market window - the interconnect move was ripe across vendors; Q3 stays partial. (3) Date/direction: the artifact (2014) precedes the parent (2017); the whitepaper's NVLink section derives generation 2 from the technology itself ('first introduced in 2016 with the Tesla P100'; the parent 'introduces the second generation of NVLink'). (4) Mediation attack: via P100, the artifact's first implementation - fails: P100 is a fellow implementer of the same artifact, and the whitepaper's derivation runs announcement -> generations, not SKU -> SKU; the design line's carrier is NVIDIA's interconnect programme, which is the node itself. Edge stands, provisional.

tsmc-16nm-finfet-plus-process-16ff-2015.name: TSMC 16nm FinFET Plus process (16FF+)
tsmc-16nm-finfet-plus-process-16ff-2015.definition: TSMC's 16nm FinFET Plus process (16FF+): the foundry transistor generation GP100 is fabricated in - 3D FinFET transistors at 16nm, in risk production by late 2014 and volume production from ~Jul 2015 (the Apple A9 generation). The P100 whitepaper names it: GP100 is 'built using TSMC's 16nm FinFET Plus process'.
tsmc-16nm-finfet-plus-process-16ff-2015.bottleneck: Before the 16nm FinFET generation, a flagship accelerator's transistor budget was capped by 28nm planar power and density, because planar scaling had ended.
tsmc-16nm-finfet-plus-process-16ff-2015.leap: TSMC's 16FF+ (volume production 2015) put FinFET transistors into volume foundry production, roughly doubling transistor density over 28nm planar and enabling 15-billion-transistor dies at datacenter power budgets.
tsmc-16nm-finfet-plus-process-16ff-2015.prior_state: Flagship GPUs (Kepler, Maxwell) were built on TSMC 28nm planar; Intel alone shipped FinFETs, in its own fabs, from 2012.

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: impossibility was scored partial at evaluation and stays partial - a reduced GP100 on 28nm is conceivable; the claim is for the parent as specified (15.3B transistors, 610 mm2, 300W), and the attack does not land beyond the partial already recorded. (2) Multiples test on Q3: Samsung's 14nm FinFET generation shipped in the same window (Exynos/Galaxy-class parts, 2015) - the FinFET generation class was multiply carried, which is exactly why Q3 is partial and why the node is the SPECIFIC process the parent's whitepaper names, not 'FinFET' as such; the node stands provisional on necessity grounds. (3) Date/direction: volume production from ~Jul 2015 (the Apple A9 generation) precedes the parent's April 2016 launch; direction is documented in the parent's own whitepaper. (4) Mediation attacks: via Intel Tri-Gate - fails as a kill: TSMC's FinFET is its own process development, not licensed Intel technology, so the phenomenon's first production carrier does not sit between TSMC's artifact and the parent; Tri-Gate is recorded as mediated via 16FF+, the correct assignment. Via the session-31 conduit finding (NVIDIA's founding fab was SGS-Thomson, TSMC entering only in 1998) - checked and does not bite: the 2016 manufacturing record names TSMC in the vendor's own whitepaper, so the conduit here is documented, not popularly assumed. No mediator named; edge stands, provisional.

cowos-silicon-interposer-packaging-tsmc-.name: CoWoS silicon-interposer packaging (TSMC)
cowos-silicon-interposer-packaging-tsmc-.definition: CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate), TSMC's 2.5D packaging platform: logic and memory dies mounted side by side on a silicon interposer whose dense wiring carries the wide memory interface. First commercial use 2011 in the Xilinx Virtex-7 2000T FPGA (first shipments 25 Oct 2011); TSMC's retrospective dates the platform's introduction to 2012 - the ambiguity is recorded, the earlier documented product date is used.
cowos-silicon-interposer-packaging-tsmc-.bottleneck: Before CoWoS, a logic die could not be wired to stacked memory across thousands of connections, because conventional package substrates cannot route a 4096-bit interface.
cowos-silicon-interposer-packaging-tsmc-.leap: TSMC's CoWoS (first commercial product 2011) productized 2.5D integration: logic and memory dies side by side on a silicon interposer, making wide-interface HBM systems manufacturable at production scale.
cowos-silicon-interposer-packaging-tsmc-.prior_state: High-performance parts shipped on organic substrates with board-routed memory interfaces a few hundred bits wide; silicon-interposer packaging was a research technique without a production platform.

sources.title: TSMC CoWoS platform records (2011- ); NVIDIA, 'NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU Architecture' whitepaper WP-08608-001_v1.1 (Aug 2017)

verification.notes: Verification of the NEW EDGE V100 -> CoWoS (the node was verified at its P100 admission). Four attacks. (1) Q1 attack: the platform's flip was 2011's; at this parent it is scored partial as the carried precondition of the package - the attack restates the score. (2) Multiples test on Q3: rival interposer/bridge offerings existed at smaller scale in the window (Intel's EMIB was announced in 2017 as a competing approach), so the platform CLASS was contested; at the parent's interface width and die size no rival was in production - Q3 stays partial. (3) Date/direction: the platform (2011) precedes the parent (2017); the parent's package (815 mm2 die + four HBM2 stacks) is an instance of it. (4) Mediation attack: via P100 - fails on the fellow-consumer discrimination: TSMC's platform is consumed by both products directly from the foundry; GP100 does not carry it into GV100. Edge stands, provisional.

openpower-foundation-2013.name: OpenPOWER Foundation
openpower-foundation-2013.definition: The OpenPOWER Foundation (formed 6 Aug 2013; founders IBM, Google, Mellanox, NVIDIA, Tyan): the consortium through which IBM opened the POWER architecture for licensing and co-development - the institutional vehicle inside which IBM opened its CPU coherence domain to partners, NVIDIA among them.
openpower-foundation-2013.bottleneck: Before the OpenPOWER Foundation, no outside accelerator maker could be given a coherent endpoint inside a major CPU line, because CPU architectures and their coherence domains were closed property with no licensing vehicle.
openpower-foundation-2013.leap: The OpenPOWER Foundation (Aug 2013) opened IBM's POWER architecture to licensing and co-development, making a CPU coherence domain a place partners could build into - the vehicle through which a GPU vendor's interconnect could terminate, coherently, inside a POWER CPU, and through which the POWER+GPU system line (S824L, Minsky, Summit/Sierra) was organised.
openpower-foundation-2013.prior_state: CPU architectures were closed: Intel refused NVIDIA a QPI licence (the 2009-2011 dispute ended NVIDIA's Intel-chipset business); IBM's POWER coherence fabric was IBM-only; accelerators attached as PCIe peripherals outside every coherence domain.

sources.title: OpenPOWER Foundation founding announcement (6 Aug 2013); NVIDIA press release, 'NVIDIA Brings Fastest Interconnect Technology to HPC and Cloud Data Centers' (GTC, 25 Mar 2014)

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: the flip survives only in its scored (partial) form - IBM had already specified coherent accelerator attach internally (CAPI, Hot Chips, the same month as the founding, Aug 2013), so what the vehicle flipped was ACCESS for non-IBM parties to a CPU coherence domain, not the existence of coherence; Q1 stays partial and the node may not be verified on Q1 grounds. (2) Multiples test on Q3: the opening move was ripe in the early 2010s - AMD's Torrenza (2006) had proposed opening a CPU fabric to accelerators, the HSA Foundation (2012) organised heterogeneous-computing standardisation, and the Open Compute Project (2011) opened server hardware; none licensed a CPU architecture or delivered a coherent GPU endpoint, but their existence caps necessity at 'ripe' - Q3 stays partial, node capped at provisional on this ground. (3) Date/direction: founded 6 Aug 2013, seven months before the parent's announcement; direction is documented in the parent's own release (IBM incorporating NVLink into future POWER CPUs; the McCredie ecosystem quote) - holds. (4) Mediation attack: via the IBM-NVIDIA POWER8 partnership (Nov 2013) - the strongest attack; it does not land as a separable milestone, because the partnership is the vehicle's own bilateral instrument, announced inside the consortium's rollout and framed in the parent's announcement as an OpenPOWER-ecosystem contribution; institutions act through their instruments without being mediated by them (the RAND-at-Bellman shape). The partnership was refused as this junction's second filing so the channel is noded exactly once; if a future design revision prefers acts over vehicles, this edge is the one to re-file. Via POWER8 - fails: the chip is the endpoint counterpart, not an intermediate the vehicle passes through. Outcome provisional.

hbm2-high-bandwidth-memory-2016.name: HBM2 high-bandwidth memory
hbm2-high-bandwidth-memory-2016.definition: HBM2 (JEDEC JESD235A, adopted Jan 2016; Samsung mass production announced 19 Jan 2016): the second-generation stacked DRAM standard - four stacks on the GPU package, 4096-bit interface, the memory technology the parent implements at 16 GB and 900 GB/s.
hbm2-high-bandwidth-memory-2016.bottleneck: Before HBM2, a GPU's memory bandwidth was capped by GDDR5-class interfaces routed through a package substrate, because no production second-generation stacked-DRAM standard existed.
hbm2-high-bandwidth-memory-2016.leap: HBM2 (2016) made stacked DRAM a production commodity - JEDEC-standardised, multi-vendor, at 720-900 GB/s beside the logic die - the memory system both the Pascal and Volta generations are built around.
hbm2-high-bandwidth-memory-2016.prior_state: GDDR5 on organic substrates (K80/M40 class, 288-480 GB/s); HBM1 (2013-15) a first generation confined to one rival product line (AMD Fiji).

sources.title: JEDEC JESD235A (Jan 2016); Samsung HBM2 mass-production announcement (19 Jan 2016); NVIDIA, 'NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU Architecture' whitepaper WP-08608-001_v1.1 (Aug 2017)

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: partially lands - HBM1 (AMD Fiji, 2015) had already shipped stacked memory at 512 GB/s, so the flip is not 'stacked memory exists' but 'a standardised, multi-vendor, second-generation production supply at 720-900 GB/s exists'; Q1's pass is recorded as resting on production-standard availability, and the node is capped at provisional on this ground. (2) Multiples test on Q3: SK Hynix's HBM2 production (2016) makes the artifact multiply supplied (it is filed as the standard-plus-production class, not Samsung's part), and the Hybrid Memory Cube was the era's rival stacked standard (refused at P100) - the stacked-memory move was contested and ripe; Q3 stays partial. (3) Date/direction: JEDEC JESD235A and Samsung mass production both Jan 2016, sixteen months before the parent; the parent implements the standard (its whitepaper's HBM2 section), direction correct. (4) Mediation attack: via P100 - the attack's best evidence is the whitepaper's own deferral ('More details of HBM2 technology are included in our Pascal Architecture Whitepaper') and its opening ('Tesla P100 was the world's first GPU architecture to support HBM2'). It fails on the fellow-consumer discrimination: a documentation pointer is not a causal carrier; the consumed artifact is the standard + the faster Samsung stacks, P100 consumed the same standard a year earlier, and the parent's memory controller is new in Volta. Edge stands, provisional. This node discharges the hearing P100 could not have (there the artifact was date-dropped as the parent's own year).

through-silicon-via-tsv-manufacturing-te.name: Through-silicon via (TSV) manufacturing technology (IBM, 2007)
through-silicon-via-tsv-manufacturing-te.definition: IBM's April 2007 announcement took TSVs from laboratory to manufacturing line: vertical connections etched through thinned silicon wafers and filled with metal, sample chips in H2 2007 and production planned for 2008, after 'more than a decade of pioneering research'.
through-silicon-via-tsv-manufacturing-te.bottleneck: Before production TSV technology, signals could not be carried vertically through a silicon wafer or carrier at manufacturing yield, because the via process existed only as laboratory demonstrations and captive prototypes.
through-silicon-via-tsv-manufacturing-te.leap: IBM's 2007 manufacturing step (with parallel productizations at Samsung and Elpida) made the through-silicon via a production process: etched, insulated, metal-filled vertical connections through thinned silicon, on a fab line.
through-silicon-via-tsv-manufacturing-te.prior_state: Vertical chip connection meant wire bonds at the die edge or flip-chip onto a substrate; TSVs were a research technique with a 1958 patent origin and 1990s consortium study.

sources.title: IBM, 'IBM Extends Moore's Law to the Third Dimension' (TSV manufacturing announcement, 12 Apr 2007)
JEDEC JESD235A (Jan 2016); Samsung HBM2 mass-production announcement (19 Jan 2016); IBM TSV announcement (Apr 2007)
IBM, 'IBM Extends Moore's Law to the Third Dimension' (12 Apr 2007)

verification.notes: Adversarial verification, session 49, parent: HBM high-bandwidth memory standard (JEDEC JESD235, 2013). This is the node's THIRD admission (CoWoS 6.5, HBM2 link 6.0, now HBM link 6.0) - TSV is now a three-child convergence node under the whole 2.5D/3D packaging subtree. MULTIPLES TEST on Q3: priced at partial permanently, per the node's standing record - Samsung WSP shipped TSV NAND from 2006 by laser drilling and Elpida completed Cu-TSV DRAM in 2009; the process class had multiple carriers and this edge does not re-litigate it. MEDIATION ATTACK 1 (via Wide I/O): Wide I/O is admitted at this same parent, and its standard device is itself TSV-stacked DRAM on an SoC - so the process is presupposed by the mediator, not transmitted through it; where both carriers are expressible, the components discrimination gives the process its own edge (the discharge pattern of HBM at HBM2, where a mediator's admission at its own level did not absorb the direct channel). Attack answered. MEDIATION ATTACK 2 (via SK Hynix's stacking craft): the first HBM chip was built by SK Hynix, so is the operative channel the partner's craft rather than the 2007 process node? The craft was heard in this expansion and recorded as mediated via the AMD programme (it reaches the standard through the partnership); the process node's claim is different in kind - it is the production existence of the via as a named, dated manufacturing step, the referent the standard's geometry presupposes for ANY implementer, not one vendor's line. Attack answered, with the boundary stated: this edge records the process class's production step, not a vendor's craft. MEDIATION ATTACK 3 (via the interposer platform - CoWoS/UMC): the standard's text is platform-neutral and its development line used UMC interposers; the platform candidates were heard in this expansion (CoWoS fail-closed partial, UMC partnership refused as formation) and neither carries the via process, which the stack's dies embody directly. Attack answered. Outcome provisional, consistent with the run's all-provisional state and with the node's two prior verification records.

ibm-silicon-carrier-packaging-knickerboc.name: IBM silicon carrier packaging (Knickerbocker et al., 2005)
ibm-silicon-carrier-packaging-knickerboc.definition: IBM's silicon-carrier system-on-package technology (CICC 2005; IBM J. Res. Dev. 49(4), 2005): multiple chips on a silicon carrier containing through-silicon vias, 50 um fine-pitch interconnection, >16x standard chip I/O and 20-100x the wiring density of traditional organic and ceramic packaging; mini-multichip modules integrating heterogeneous dies into a single 'virtual chip'.
ibm-silicon-carrier-packaging-knickerboc.bottleneck: Before the silicon carrier, multiple dies could not be wired together at lithographic density on a shared carrier, because organic and ceramic substrates route at 20-100x coarser pitch.
ibm-silicon-carrier-packaging-knickerboc.leap: Knickerbocker et al. (2005) demonstrated and characterized the silicon carrier: production dies mounted on a TSV-bearing silicon wafer used purely as a wiring medium, at 50 um interconnection pitch - the 2.5D architecture in published, quantified form.
ibm-silicon-carrier-packaging-knickerboc.prior_state: Multichip modules on glass-ceramic or organic laminate carriers; silicon interposers a scattered research topic without a characterized platform publication.

sources.title: Knickerbocker et al., 'Three dimensional silicon integration using fine pitch interconnection, silicon processing and silicon carrier packaging technology' (CICC 2005); IBM J. Res. Dev. 49(4), 2005

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: silicon-carrier and interposer research existed at other laboratories in the same years (European and US packaging groups), so 'no demonstrated architecture before 2005' is too strong in the abstract; the node survives as scoped - the published, quantified characterization with production dies (>16x I/O, 20-100x wiring density, 50 um pitch) is the form the lineage cites. (2) Multiples test on Q3 LANDS partially and is already priced at partial: parallel interposer programmes existed, and TSMC's own line might have converged independently through the SSI co-development - this is the expansion's MOST CONTESTABLE edge. Re-hearing condition: a document showing TSMC's interposer programme derived its architecture from a different named source, or that the SSI design work proceeded in documented ignorance of the carrier literature, reopens this edge. (3) Date and direction: CICC September 2005 and IBM J. Res. Dev. 49(4) 2005 are defensible; direction architecture -> platform is correct. (4) Mediation attacks: via Xilinx SSI - answered (SSI is refused at this parent on identity grounds as the parent's own first form, and the carrier predates it by five years on an independent IBM lineage); via TSV - answered (containment of a component is not mediation of the architecture's channel; components discrimination). No mediation object recorded. Outcome provisional.

hbm-high-bandwidth-memory-standard-jedec.name: HBM high-bandwidth memory standard (JEDEC JESD235, 2013)
hbm-high-bandwidth-memory-standard-jedec.definition: The first-generation High Bandwidth Memory standard (JEDEC JESD235, adopted Oct 2013; developed by AMD with SK Hynix from their 2010 JEDEC proposal; first chip built by SK Hynix in 2013; first product AMD Fiji, June 2015): four stacked DRAM dies on a base logic die, a 1024-bit interface, 128 GB/s per stack at 1 Gb/s per pin.
hbm-high-bandwidth-memory-standard-jedec.bottleneck: Before HBM, no standard existed for a stacked-DRAM wide interface, because graphics and HPC memory still crossed a circuit board on narrow, power-hungry channels (GDDR5) and the stacked alternative existed only as vendor experiments (Wide I/O for mobile, HMC as a proprietary-leaning cube).
hbm-high-bandwidth-memory-standard-jedec.leap: HBM (2013) defined the stacked-DRAM wide interface as a multi-vendor standard: four TSV-stacked dies on a base logic die presenting 1024 bits at 128 GB/s per stack - the architecture every later HBM generation revises.
hbm-high-bandwidth-memory-standard-jedec.prior_state: GDDR5 board-level memory as the graphics standard; Wide I/O (2011) as a mobile-only stacked standard without a graphics/HPC product.

sources.title: Wikipedia, 'High Bandwidth Memory' (history and development sections)

verification.notes: Four attacks run. (1) Q1 attack: HBM was not the only stacked-memory standard of 2013 - HMC's Specification 1.0 is the same year, and Wide I/O predates both. The attack does not land on the node as scoped: its claim is the wide-interface standard (raw 1024-bit parallel interface, base die as buffer), the form the parent revises; HMC is recorded at this expansion as the rival/multiple, not a co-carrier. (2) Multiples test on Q3 LANDS and is already priced at partial: Wide I/O's channels and HMC's stack were parallel carriers of the stacked idea, so a second-generation standard could in principle have been revised from a different first generation; the parent's actual text is JESD235's revision, which is what the edge records. (3) Mediation attacks: via the JEDEC process - answered (the process was refused at this parent on self-carriage: the parent IS a JEDEC document, and a document-to-document revision needs no institutional conduit); via the AMD development programme - answered (refused on own-formation; the programme's separable artifacts were heard directly). The fellow-consumer discrimination from session 47 is preserved: P100 does not mediate this edge - both products consume the standard, and the parent here is the standard's own revision. (4) Date and direction: JESD235 adopted Oct 2013 (JEDEC record, Wikipedia history); direction first generation -> revision is documentary (JESD235A amends JESD235). Outcome provisional.

bosch-process-deep-reactive-ion-etching-.name: Bosch process deep reactive-ion etching (Laermer & Schilp, 1994)
bosch-process-deep-reactive-ion-etching-.definition: The Bosch process (Laermer & Schilp at Robert Bosch; German priority Dec 1992, DE 4241045 published 1994, US 5,501,893 granted 1996) etches deep, near-vertical holes in silicon by alternating SF6 etch cycles with C4F8 sidewall-passivation cycles, at >2 um/min with >100:1 mask selectivity - the process that made high-aspect-ratio silicon etching a fab recipe, developed for MEMS sensors.
bosch-process-deep-reactive-ion-etching-.bottleneck: Before the Bosch process, deep holes could not be etched vertically into silicon at production rates, because plasma etching either undercut the mask laterally or stalled at shallow depth, and wet etching followed the crystal planes.
bosch-process-deep-reactive-ion-etching-.leap: The Bosch cycle split silicon etching in time - alternating etch and passivation steps - and made deep, vertical, high-aspect-ratio structures a routine fab recipe: first the MEMS sensor industry, then every etched through-silicon via.
bosch-process-deep-reactive-ion-etching-.prior_state: Deep silicon structures were made by anisotropic wet etching (crystal-plane-limited KOH) or slow, shallow reactive-ion etching; vertical-walled holes tens of microns deep were laboratory work.

sources.title: Laermer & Urban, 'Bosch-DRIE Shaping MEMS - History, Applications and Future Directions', Hilton Head Workshop 2010

verification.notes: Adversarial verification, session 49, parent: Through-silicon via (TSV) manufacturing technology (IBM, 2007). This edge discharges the hearing assigned at the CoWoS expansion (session 48: DRIE fail-closed partial at CoWoS, 'its hearing belongs to the TSV node's expansion'). MULTIPLES TEST on Q3: lands and is priced at partial in the stored evaluation. The multiples are INSIDE etch technology - cryogenic single-step deep etching (Jansen et al.) was a parallel production route, and laser drilling formed Samsung WSP's vias by another mechanism entirely - so the Bosch cycle was the production default, not the only conceivable path; Q3 cannot rise above partial on this record. MEDIATION ATTACK 1 (via STS equipment): the recipe is wielded through machines, but the TSV fabrication literature names the RECIPE ('once the via is made by DRIE' - Lau; IBM's own process overview, Andry et al., names deep reactive ion etching for IBM's via-middle flow), and the recipe is a separable, licensed, patented artifact (US 5,501,893) that predates and is independent of any tool vendor. Recipe-over-equipment discrimination; the STS system itself was evaluated in the same expansion and failed closed partial (equipment carrier, no documented IBM installation). Attack answered. MEDIATION ATTACK 2 (via the fill steps - superfilling / damascene): the via is etched BEFORE it is filled; the etch channel is separable from the fill channel, and both fill candidates were heard on their own records in the same expansion (both fail-closed partial). Attack answered. MEDIATION ATTACK 3 (via the parent itself - 'IBM's process integration is the real enabler'): circular by construction; the parent's leap is the integration, and this edge records the integration's presupposed process step - the same shape as TSV's own admission at CoWoS. Attack answered. HONESTY CAVEAT, recorded in full: IBM's April 2007 announcement does NOT name its etch recipe - it says the vias are 'etched through the silicon wafer'. The identification of the etch as the Bosch process rests on (a) the generic TSV fabrication literature (Lau's sequence), (b) IBM Research's own TSV overview naming DRIE, and (c) the Bosch process's status as the era's only production deep-silicon etch (STS shipped the first commercial systems in 1995 as Bosch's licensee; the process was 'the industrial workhorse'). If a document emerges showing IBM's 2007 line etched its vias by a non-Bosch route (e.g. a captive cryogenic process), this edge's Q1/Q11 evidence must be re-heard; that is the re-hearing condition for this record. Outcome provisional - consistent with the run's all-provisional state and with the identification resting on the literature rather than the parent's own text.

wide-i-o-mobile-dram-standard-jedec-jesd.name: Wide I/O mobile DRAM standard (JEDEC JESD229, 2011)
wide-i-o-mobile-dram-standard-jedec-jesd.definition: JEDEC's Wide I/O Single Data Rate standard (JESD229, Dec 2011): the first JEDEC standard for TSV-stacked DRAM - a 512-bit interface of four independent 128-bit channels, SDR clocking to 266 MHz, 17 GB/s, 1.2V signalling, DRAM dies stacked directly on a mobile SoC. Wikipedia's HBM article calls JESD229 'the predecessor of HBM' and records that JESD235 'followed' it.
wide-i-o-mobile-dram-standard-jedec-jesd.bottleneck: Before Wide I/O, TSV-stacked DRAM existed only as vendor-proprietary productizations, because no multi-vendor interface specification existed for a DRAM stack - each stack was one company's captive design, and no second vendor could build to it.
wide-i-o-mobile-dram-standard-jedec-jesd.leap: Wide I/O made the TSV-stacked DRAM a standard object: four independent 128-bit channels over through-silicon vias at mobile power - the channel architecture the HBM lineage inherits, doubles per die and re-clocks.
wide-i-o-mobile-dram-standard-jedec-jesd.prior_state: Stacked memory meant wire-bonded MCPs or proprietary TSV stacks (Samsung WSP, Elpida's Cu-TSV DRAM); mobile memory was LPDDR2 on a board.

sources.title: IFTLE 87, 'JEDEC Wide IO stds...' (Semiconductor Digest, Jan 2012)

verification.notes: Adversarial verification, session 49, parent: HBM high-bandwidth memory standard (JEDEC JESD235, 2013). This edge discharges the hearing assigned at the HBM2 expansion (session 48: Wide I/O mediated via HBM, 'its direct hearing belongs to HBM's expansion'), discharged as an ADMISSION. ion-assisted-plasma-etching-mechanism-co.name: Ion-assisted plasma etching mechanism (Coburn & Winters, 1979)
ion-assisted-plasma-etching-mechanism-co.definition: Coburn and Winters at IBM San Jose showed in 1979 - with xenon difluoride and a directed ion beam, outside any plasma - that ion bombardment and fluorine chemistry together etch silicon far faster than the sum of either alone, and directionally; their mechanism papers (J. Vac. Sci. Technol. 16:391; J. Appl. Phys. 50:3189) are the founding explanation of ion-enhanced etching.
ion-assisted-plasma-etching-mechanism-co.bottleneck: Before Coburn & Winters, plasma etching could not be designed for direction, because fluorine chemistry etched silicon spontaneously in all directions and the contribution of ion bombardment to a surface reaction had never been isolated from the chemistry it assists.
ion-assisted-plasma-etching-mechanism-co.leap: Coburn & Winters isolated the ion-assisted etching mechanism: an ion beam aimed at a silicon surface under XeF2 etched far faster than chemistry or sputtering alone - the directional engine inside every subsequent anisotropic plasma etch, and the mechanism the Bosch cycle's etch step runs on.
ion-assisted-plasma-etching-mechanism-co.prior_state: Plasma etching was empirical: isotropic chemical attack or slow physical sputtering, with anisotropy an unexplained property of particular recipes (reactive ion etching, 1974) rather than a mechanism that could be designed around.

sources.title: Academic Jobs / DRIE history feature, 'Deep reactive ion etching: top researchers who got us here'

verification.notes: Adversarial verification, session 50 expansion 1 (DRIE). MULTIPLES TEST on Q3: the ion-assisted effect was embodied empirically in RIE practice (Hosokawa 1974) five years before its explanation, and parallel mechanism work existed in the late-1970s plasma community - Q3 stays partial, honestly. The edge does not rest on the parent citing the paper: US 5,501,893 does not name Coburn & Winters. The channel is instantiation - the patent's claims require ion bombardment during the etch steps to clear the floor polymer, which is the 1979 mechanism in functional language, and the mechanism has a unique founding artifact pair (JVST 16:391; J. Appl. Phys. 50:3189) demonstrated reactor-independently (XeF2 + ion beam), so it is not the RIE apparatus wearing another name. This is the Quetelet shape: instantiation of a mechanism with a unique founding artifact carries a channel even without a name. MEDIATION ATTACK: is the mechanism itself mediated via RIE (1974)? No - the direction runs the other way and is recorded on the RIE candidate (mediated via this node): the 1974 report instantiated the effect without explaining it; the 1979 work is the cited final link for the mechanism. No re-hearing condition attaches to this edge beyond the general one: a document showing the parent's etch step designed on a different stated mechanism would reopen it.

copper-damascene-interconnect-technology.name: Copper damascene interconnect technology (IBM, 1997)
copper-damascene-interconnect-technology.definition: IBM's copper damascene back-end-of-line process (1997) - copper wiring electroplated into etched dielectric trenches, replacing aluminium - the BEOL technology whose design rules and fine-pitch Cu wiring the parent's carrier fabrication follows.
copper-damascene-interconnect-technology.bottleneck: Before damascene, copper could not be used for fine on-chip or on-carrier wiring, because copper cannot be plasma-etched like aluminium and diffuses lethally into silicon and its dielectrics - the best conductor was unusable in the fab.
copper-damascene-interconnect-technology.leap: IBM's copper damascene process inverted interconnect patterning - etch trenches in the dielectric, electroplate copper in, polish back, barrier the metal - making copper the production interconnect and turning back-end-of-line into a transferable high-density wiring capability that a package substrate could then be built with.
copper-damascene-interconnect-technology.prior_state: Interconnect was subtractively etched aluminium, its resistance-capacitance delay rising as wires shrank; copper was known to be better and known to be unmanufacturable.

c4-controlled-collapse-chip-connection-m.name: C4 controlled-collapse chip connection (Miller, 1969)
c4-controlled-collapse-chip-connection-m.definition: IBM's controlled-collapse chip connection: the flip-chip solder joint whose collapse is limited by glass dams defining the solderable area, published by Miller (IBM J. Res. Dev. 13(3), May 1969) with companion reliability and geometry papers in the same issue; the practice descends from IBM's summer-1962 reduction to practice of the glass-passivated solder-bump flip chip (3 bumps per chip, copper-ball standoff), and placing bumps over active device area is what created the area array.
c4-controlled-collapse-chip-connection-m.bottleneck: Before C4, a chip's connections left from its edges - wire bonds placed one at a time around the periphery - so I/O count grew with perimeter while silicon capability grew with area.
c4-controlled-collapse-chip-connection-m.leap: Controlled-collapse chip connection put solder bumps over the whole face of the chip, their collapse governed by surface tension against glass-dam-defined pads, joining every I/O in a single reflow - the area array, which let interconnection scale with die area instead of die perimeter.
c4-controlled-collapse-chip-connection-m.prior_state: Peripheral wire bonding and beam leads: serial, pitch-bound, inductance-heavy interconnection, one wire at a time.

chemical-mechanical-planarization-ibm-19.name: Chemical-mechanical planarization (IBM, 1983)
chemical-mechanical-planarization-ibm-19.definition: IBM's chemical-mechanical planarization process (first semiconductor planarization experiments at IBM East Fishkill, 1983; a named process sector from 1988) - pad-and-slurry polishing that restores a wafer surface to planarity and, applied to metal, removes overburden selectively.
chemical-mechanical-planarization-ibm-19.bottleneck: Before chemical-mechanical planarization, multilevel wiring topography was impractical to flatten and deposited metal could not be removed selectively, because each added level compounded surface relief beyond lithography's depth of focus and no fab step could polish a wafer back to planarity.
chemical-mechanical-planarization-ibm-19.leap: CMP (IBM, from the 1983 East Fishkill planarization experiments; a named production process from the late 1980s) turned polishing into a precision fab step - pad, slurry and chemistry removing material selectively and restoring planarity between levels - and later supplied the removal step that makes inlaid (damascene) metal patterning possible at all.
chemical-mechanical-planarization-ibm-19.prior_state: Planarization ran on spin-on glass, dielectric etchback and reflow; topography accumulated across levels and capped practical multilevel wiring, and metal removal meant etching the metal itself.

sources.title: Fury, Milestones in a Quarter Century of CMP, ECS Trans. 19(7) (2009); CMP: Four Decades of Innovation, ECS Meeting Abstracts (2024)

Q3 stays partial as scored in evaluation (etchback counterfactual), so the node is not verified on necessity grounds.
